I tried to use cp.inf and cp.nan in jit.rawkernel, but get error: identifier "inf" is undefined. I find previous issue  #7118, and it has been fixed in #7122. but jit.rawkernel still havs this problem.

### Reproduce

```python
from cupyx import jit
import cupy as cp


@jit.rawkernel()
def test_inf_nan(arr):
    idx = jit.threadIdx.x + jit.blockDim.x * jit.blockIdx.x
    if idx == 0:
        arr[0] = cp.inf
        arr[0] = cp.nan
        arr[0] = 0

print(test_inf_nan[5,5](cp.linspace(0,4,10)))
``` 

Then it gives the following errors:
```
error: identifier "inff" is undefined
      arr[0] = (double)(inff);
                        ^

error: invalid type conversion
      arr[0] = (double)(nanf);

  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). * I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .

* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

when trying to create a CuPy array with pinned memory we get a Type Error.

`TypeError: Cannot convert cupy.cuda.pinned_memory.PinnedMemoryPointer to cupy.cuda.memory.MemoryPointer`

### To Reproduce

```py
import cupy

with cupy.cuda.using_allocator(cupy.get_default_pinned_memory_pool().malloc):
    a = cupy.arange(10)
```

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

Hi,

I have two nodes (each with 1 GPU, and both IB + Ethernet NICs). I'm trying to create two communicators, one for IB and one for Ethernet, respectively. The environment variable changes only seem to affect the first communicator.

I tried to use cp.inf and cp.nan in jit.rawkernel, but get error: identifier "inf" is undefined. I find previous issue  #7118, and it has been fixed in #7122. but jit.rawkernel still havs this problem.

### Reproduce

```python
from cupyx import jit
import cupy as cp


@jit.rawkernel()
def test_inf_nan(arr):
    idx = jit.threadIdx.x + jit.blockDim.x * jit.blockIdx.x
    if idx == 0:
        arr[0] = cp.inf
        arr[0] = cp.nan
        arr[0] = 0

print(test_inf_nan[5,5](cp.linspace(0,4,10)))
``` 

Then it gives the following errors:
```
error: identifier "inff" is undefined
      arr[0] = (double)(inff);
                        ^

error: invalid type conversion
      arr[0] = (double)(nanf);

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2).  The tests indirectly cover Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). * The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2).  The tests indirectly cover implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2).  The tests indirectly cover implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). This is very tricky as I keep revisiting this part, and I'd like to share my understanding here to aid code review.

When this `toDlpack()` function was called, the producer/consumer streams are ordered, that's why we did not need to pass any stream argument. 

This is no longer true when CPU copy is requested. In the case of NumPy, [`stream=None` is provided](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/816fd7c0d1569bef00b3765d47528b093cf55839/numpy/_core/src/multiarray/dlpack.c#L536), but CuPy turns it to `streamLegacy` in `__dlpack__` and orders it after CuPy's current stream (whatever it is), so we're now on the consumer's (legacy) stream. We need a way to pass this info to `get(stream=consumer_stream, order='A')` to make a blocking copy of the array on the legacy stream to CPU. The easiest way to ensure correctness is to pass it through `toDLPack()`. Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .

* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

implements dlpack version 1 and cleans up some of the error handling a little bit.

Some notes:
* I did not add support for `from_dlpack(..., dl_device!=None)`, because the main point of that is currently .
* We support device requests if the device matches exactly _or_ when the request is to copy to the CPU.
* I grudgingly ignore the readonly flag right now on import, because we may need a way to ignore it.  To some degree, I think this is a producer problem (i.e. a project that produces read-only, should maybe provide a way to get a writeable version or ignore it).
  The reason is basically: This can be deprecated easily enough at some point, but I dunno if it may be a regression.
* The UnitTest/pytest interaction confused the heck out of me, so I replaced everything with fixtures.

I think the tests cover things fairly well, although of course not cleanup in the CPU exposing path.  I am not too worried about that, though.
EDIT: Another untested point is that we set the `IS_COPIED` flag when we copied to CPU.

This means that `np.from_dlpack(cupy_arr, device="cpu")` works (with NumPy 2). NumPy has a [`numpy.linalg.eigvals`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.eigvals.html) function, which is often used in real-life programs.

Description
I tried to use jit.rawkernel to do some complex calculation, but the result have some small errors. The following code gives an example. I have explicitly specified the data type as complex128.

### Reproduce
```python
from cupyx import jit
import cupy as cp
from numba import cuda
import numpy as np


@jit.rawkernel()
def cupy_test(y):
    tid = jit.blockIdx.x * jit.blockDim.x + jit.threadIdx.x
    wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
    for j in range(734):
        y[tid] += cp.complex128(wavek * 1.0j)


@cuda.jit
def numba_test(y):
    tid = cuda.blockIdx.x * cuda.blockDim.x + cuda.threadIdx.x
    wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
    for j in range(734):
        y[tid] += complex(0, wavek)


size = 32 * 32
x = cp.empty((size,), dtype=cp.complex128)
x[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j
y = np.empty((size,), dtype=np.complex128)
y[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j
z = np.empty((size,), dtype=np.complex128)
z[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j

cupy_test[32,32](x)
numba_test[32,32](y)

wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6

I tried to use jit.rawkernel to do some complex calculation, but the result have some small errors. The following code gives an example. I have explicitly specified the data type as complex128.

### Reproduce
```python
from cupyx import jit
import cupy as cp
from numba import cuda
import numpy as np


@jit.rawkernel()
def cupy_test(y):
    tid = jit.blockIdx.x * jit.blockDim.x + jit.threadIdx.x
    wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
    for j in range(734):
        y[tid] += cp.complex128(wavek * 1.0j)


@cuda.jit
def numba_test(y):
    tid = cuda.blockIdx.x * cuda.blockDim.x + cuda.threadIdx.x
    wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
    for j in range(734):
        y[tid] += complex(0, wavek)


size = 32 * 32
x = cp.empty((size,), dtype=cp.complex128)
x[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j
y = np.empty((size,), dtype=np.complex128)
y[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j
z = np.empty((size,), dtype=np.complex128)
z[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j

cupy_test[32,32](x)
numba_test[32,32](y)

wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
for i in range(734):
    z[:] += cp.complex128(wavek * 1.j)

print("For cupy-kernel, the result is {}".format(x[0]))
print("For numba, the result is {}".format(y[0]))
print("For cupy, the result is {}".format(z[0]))
print("The real result is {}".format(wavek * 734 * 1.j))
``` 

Then the output is
```Plaintext
For cupy-kernel, the result is -3074572043.5j
For numba, the result is -3074571957.8666654j
For cupy, the result is -3074571957.8666654j
The real result is (-0-3074571957.866667j)
```

I tried to use jit.rawkernel to do some complex calculation, but the result have some small errors. The following code gives an example. I have explicitly specified the data type as complex128.

### Reproduce
```python
from cupyx import jit
import cupy as cp
from numba import cuda
import numpy as np


@jit.rawkernel()
def cupy_test(y):
    tid = jit.blockIdx.x * jit.blockDim.x + jit.threadIdx.x
    wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
    for j in range(734):
        y[tid] += cp.complex128(wavek * 1.0j)


@cuda.jit
def numba_test(y):
    tid = cuda.blockIdx.x * cuda.blockDim.x + cuda.threadIdx.x
    wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
    for j in range(734):
        y[tid] += complex(0, wavek)


size = 32 * 32
x = cp.empty((size,), dtype=cp.complex128)
x[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j
y = np.empty((size,), dtype=np.complex128)
y[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j
z = np.empty((size,), dtype=np.complex128)
z[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j

cupy_test[32,32](x)
numba_test[32,32](y)

wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
for i in range(734):
    z[:] += cp.complex128(wavek * 1.j)

print("For cupy-kernel, the result is {}".format(x[0]))
print("For numba, the result is {}".format(y[0]))
print("For cupy, the result is {}".format(z[0]))
print("The real result is {}".format(wavek * 734 * 1.j))
``` 

Then the output is
```Plaintext
For cupy-kernel, the result is -3074572043.5j
For numba, the result is -3074571957.8666654j
For cupy, the result is -3074571957.8666654j
The real result is (-0-3074571957.866667j)
```

I tried to use jit.rawkernel to do some complex calculation, but the result have some small errors. The following code gives an example. I have explicitly specified the data type as complex128.

### Reproduce
```python
from cupyx import jit
import cupy as cp
from numba import cuda
import numpy as np


@jit.rawkernel()
def cupy_test(y):
    tid = jit.blockIdx.x * jit.blockDim.x + jit.threadIdx.x
    wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
    for j in range(734):
        y[tid] += cp.complex128(wavek * 1.0j)


@cuda.jit
def numba_test(y):
    tid = cuda.blockIdx.x * cuda.blockDim.x + cuda.threadIdx.x
    wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
    for j in range(734):
        y[tid] += complex(0, wavek)


size = 32 * 32
x = cp.empty((size,), dtype=cp.complex128)
x[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j
y = np.empty((size,), dtype=np.complex128)
y[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j
z = np.empty((size,), dtype=np.complex128)
z[:] = 0.0 + 0.0j

cupy_test[32,32](x)
numba_test[32,32](y)

wavek = -2 * 3.1415926 / 1.5e-6
for i in range(734):
    z[:] += cp.complex128(wavek * 1.j)

`numpy.rint` returns either a ndarray or scalar from: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.rint.html#numpy.rint
but cupy returns a `cupy.ndarray`, is this expected?

```shell
> python test.py
<class 'numpy.int64'>
<class 'cupy.ndarray'>
[1647 8534 1848 ... 3270 1723  957]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/fedemengo/workspace/test/test.py", line 16, in <module>
    xp_ii = xp.random.choice(xp_a, size, replace=False)
  File "/home/fedemengo/workspace/test/venv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/cupy/random/_sample.py", line 190, in choice
    return rs.choice(a, size, replace, p)
  File "/home/fedemengo/workspace/test/venv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/cupy/random/_generator.py", line 1091, in choice
    raise NotImplementedError
NotImplementedError
```

### To Reproduce

```py
> cat test.py
import numpy as np
import cupy as xp

a = 9128
size = 8256

nn_a = np.rint(a).astype(int)
xp_a = xp.rint(a).astype(int)

print(type(nn_a))
print(type(xp_a))

np_ii = np.random.choice(nn_a, size, replace=False)
print(np_ii)

xp_ii = xp.random.choice(xp_a, size, replace=False)
print(xp_ii)
```

Wheel (`pip install cupy-***`)

seems that I have found some kind of a strange memory allocation bug. I am running Debian testing, which hast cuda 11.2 and cython 29.21. So I had to build cupy ("pip3 install cupy" - no errors reported except missing cudnn/cublas etc).

Now, the problem is that I wanted to benchmark memory transfer between host memory and device memory. In general, this is nothing more than measuring the timing of many transfers of the same array. So memory allocation had to be really negligible, but with cupy it is not. It is growing until it gets killed by OOM-killer. I had the similar test in Numba without any problems. 

Here is a simplified code that triggers such behavior on my PC (quite an old Xeon E3-1220 with 16Gb DDR3 memory, python 3.9.1).  If there is no explicit release of memory buffers, the memory occupied by python grows steadily. Actually it should not. I have added a small time delay to the cycle to be able to observe this behavior and found another strange thing. If time delay is longer than 0.2s (I suspect that the value depends on the hardware), then the memory occupation gets capped at 3.4 Gb and test passes. For comparison, with pinned_mempool.free_all_blocks() memory occupation remains at the level around 2.4Gb. 

It seems to me, that there is some automatic garbage collection which can not cope with a rate that this test allocates/deallocates pinned memory. But works to at least some extent, if the rate is decreased by addition of sufficient sleeping time. Since I do not observe such problem with Numba on the same configuration, I guess that this bug is not in linux/python/cuda stack but rather in cupy itself.  



```
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp
import time

N = 10*1024*1024

cpu_data = np.zeros(N, dtype=np.float32)

mempool = cp.get_default_memory_pool()
pinned_mempool = cp.get_default_pinned_memory_pool()

for i in range(5000):
    gpu_data = cp.asarray(cpu_data)

    if i % 100 == 0:
        print(i, mempool.used_bytes(), mempool.total_bytes(), pinned_mempool.n_free_blocks())    

        time.sleep(0.1)
        #pinned_mempool.free_all_blocks()

print("Ok")

```

```

>>> _environment._get_include_dir_from_conda_or_wheel(12, 5)
['/home/dagardner/work/conda/envs/morpheus/targets/-linux/include', '/home/dagardner/work/conda/envs/morpheus/include']
```

One possible work-around would be to call `platform.machine()` on systems that return an empty string:
```
>>> import platform
>>> platform.processor()
''
>>> platform.machine()
'x86_64'
```

Description

In the scipy's implementation of svds we can get the number of singular values to be at max equal to min(M,N) using propack solver. I needed this particular implementation in the cupy's version of svds (where kmax is mandatorily lesser then min(M,N) )for a project that I am working in IIT Bombay's structure lab.

Can anyone guide me how to add this?

Check the scipy's implementation:

believe the issue is that `platform.processor()` returns an empty string on some systems (https://docs.python.org/3.10/library/platform.html#platform.processor), and as such on my machine in a Conda env the `cupy._environment._get_include_dir_from_conda_or_wheel` method returns an invalid path:
```
>>> from cupy import _environment
>>> _environment._get_include_dir_from_conda_or_wheel(12, 5)
['/home/dagardner/work/conda/envs/morpheus/targets/-linux/include', '/home/dagardner/work/conda/envs/morpheus/include']
```

One possible work-around would be to call `platform.machine()` on systems that return an empty string:
```
>>> import platform
>>> platform.processor()
''
>>> platform.machine()
'x86_64'
```

```
import cupy as cp
cp.array(cp.zeros((1,)))
```

['/home/dagardner/work/conda/envs/morpheus/targets/-linux/include', '/home/dagardner/work/conda/envs/morpheus/include']
```

One possible work-around would be to call `platform.machine()` on systems that return an empty string:
```
>>> import platform
>>> platform.processor()
''
>>> platform.machine()
'x86_64'

# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run
* Make sure to cover the new Distutils C++ compilers

# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). # Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run

# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run
* Make sure to cover the new Distutils C++ compilers

Description

In the scipy's implementation of svds we can get the number of singular values to be at max equal to min(M,N) using propack solver. I needed this particular implementation in the cupy's version of svds (where kmax is mandatorily lesser then min(M,N) )for a project that I am working in IIT Bombay's structure lab.

Can anyone guide me how to add this?

Check the scipy's implementation:

Description

I tried to compile cupy with the rocm libraries that Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS provides in its default package sources. This did not work because the cupy build tool chain was not able to find hipblas. Listed below are all the files that are installed with `libhipblas-dev` and `libhipblas0`. I tested both, not setting `ROCM_HOME` at all and setting it to `/usr`. In both cases cupy could not find hipblas.

```
$ dpkg -L libhipblas-dev
/.
/usr
/usr/include
/usr/include/hipblas
/usr/include/hipblas/hipblas-export.h
/usr/include/hipblas/hipblas-version.h
/usr/include/hipblas/hipblas.h
/usr/lib
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/cmake
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/cmake/hipblas
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/cmake/hipblas/hipblas-config-version.cmake
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/cmake/hipblas/hipblas-config.cmake
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/cmake/hipblas/hipblas-targets-release.cmake
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/cmake/hipblas/hipblas-targets.cmake
/usr/share
/usr/share/doc
/usr/share/doc/libhipblas-dev
/usr/share/doc/libhipblas-dev/copyright
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libhipblas.so
/usr/share/doc/libhipblas-dev/changelog.Debian.gz
$ dpkg -L libhipblas0
/.
/usr
/usr/lib
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libhipblas.so.0.1
/usr/share
/usr/share/doc
/usr/share/doc/libhipblas0
/usr/share/doc/libhipblas0/changelog.Debian.gz
/usr/share/doc/libhipblas0/copyright
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libhipblas.so.0

```

```[tasklist]
## Planned Features
- [ ] #8306
- [ ] `complex32` support for limited APIs (restart [#4454](https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/4454))
- [ ] Support bfloat16
- [ ] Structured Data Type
- [ ] Allow using CUDA libraries installed as Python modules (#8013)
- [ ] pyproject.toml support (#6986)
- [ ] Drop support for Python 3.9 following [SPEC 0](https://scientific-python.org/specs/spec-0000/)
```

```[tasklist]
## Timeline & Release Manager
- [ ] **v14.0.0a1** (TBD)
- [ ] **v14.0.0b1** (TBD)
- [ ] **v14.0.0rc1** (TBD)
- [ ] **v14.0.0** (TBD)
```

## Notes

* Starting in the CuPy v13 development cycle, we have adjusted our release frequency to once every two months. Mid-term or hot-fix releases may be provided depending on necessity, such as for new CUDA/Python version support or critical bug fixes.
* The schedule and planned features may be subject to change depending on the progress of the development.
* `v13.x` releases will only contain backported pull-requests (mainly bug-fixes) from the v14 (`main`) branch.

## Past Release Plans

* v9: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/3891
* v10: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/5049
