# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run
* Make sure to cover the new Distutils C++ compilers

v74.0 (specifically https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4600) removed `setuptools.msvc` module, which has been there for 8 years. * build-time: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/69a2137ec7577adb03407ed3e8db373ee2118b4c/install/cupy_builder/_compiler.py#L265-L266
* runtime (Windows only): https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/69a2137ec7577adb03407ed3e8db373ee2118b4c/cupy/cuda/compiler.py#L102

Until the problem is resolved, we will pin the setuptools version in the CI. (#8567)

### Workarounds (for users)

* Windows users seeing `Failed to auto-detect cl.exe path` warning: Do one of the following workarounds:
    1. Downgrade setuptools to v73.x or earlier
    2. Upgrade setuptools to v74.1.0 or later, and do `import setuptools.msvc` along with `import cupy`
    3. Manually add `cl.exe` directory (e.g., `C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2019\BuildTools\VC\Tools\MSVC\14.29.30133\bin\HostX86\x64\`) to `PATH`
* Linux/Windows users experiencing `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'setuptools.msvc'` error when building CuPy from source: This problems happens with setuptools v74.0.0 only. Try upgrading setuptools to v74.1.0 or later (or downgrade setuptools to v73.x or earlier).

Both problems will be fixed in the future release (#8583).

Follows-up #8574. Reverts #8567.

edit: This PR adopts recent setuptools changes, specifically v74.0.0 (which [removed](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4600) `setuptools.msvc`) and v74.1.0+ (which [reverted](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4626) `setuptools.msvc` but requires explicit module import instead of `import setuptools`).

<details>
<summary>Original description</summary>

On Windows platform with setuptools 74+, it will now take 2-3 seconds to find `cl.exe`. This overhead happens only once per process, and only when the use of `nvcc` is requested.

`setuptools.msvc` (which we rely on for years and is now removed) was able to discover `cl.exe` very quickly as it directly reads the Windows registry. The new approach introduced in this PR (which only uses the public/documented setuptools API) retrives the compiler path through `vcvarsall.bat`, which incurs subprocess invocation.

edit: This PR adopts recent setuptools changes, specifically v74.0.0 (which [removed](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4600) `setuptools.msvc`) and v74.1.0+ (which [reverted](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4626) `setuptools.msvc` but requires explicit module import instead of `import setuptools`).

<details>
<summary>Original description</summary>

On Windows platform with setuptools 74+, it will now take 2-3 seconds to find `cl.exe`. This overhead happens only once per process, and only when the use of `nvcc` is requested.

`setuptools.msvc` (which we rely on for years and is now removed) was able to discover `cl.exe` very quickly as it directly reads the Windows registry. The new approach introduced in this PR (which only uses the public/documented setuptools API) retrives the compiler path through `vcvarsall.bat`, which incurs subprocess invocation.

When I try to use the random seed with a integer random seed
I get the error 
```
TypeError: Cannot cast scalar from dtype('int64') to dtype('uint64') according to the rule 'safe'
```


### To Reproduce

```py
import cupy as cp
print("cupy version: ",cp.__version__):
cp.random.seed(0)
```


### Installation

None

### Environment

```
print("cupy version: ",cp.__version__):
cupy version:  13.2.0
```


### Additional Information

You can solve this problem by converting the integer to an unsigned integer, either internally or like this

```
import cupy as cp
import ctypes
random_seed = 0;
cp.random.seed(ctypes.c_ulong(random_seed ))
```

seems that I have found some kind of a strange memory allocation bug. I am running Debian testing, which hast cuda 11.2 and cython 29.21. So I had to build cupy ("pip3 install cupy" - no errors reported except missing cudnn/cublas etc).

Now, the problem is that I wanted to benchmark memory transfer between host memory and device memory. In general, this is nothing more than measuring the timing of many transfers of the same array. So memory allocation had to be really negligible, but with cupy it is not. It is growing until it gets killed by OOM-killer. I had the similar test in Numba without any problems. 

Here is a simplified code that triggers such behavior on my PC (quite an old Xeon E3-1220 with 16Gb DDR3 memory, python 3.9.1).  If there is no explicit release of memory buffers, the memory occupied by python grows steadily. Actually it should not. I have added a small time delay to the cycle to be able to observe this behavior and found another strange thing. If time delay is longer than 0.2s (I suspect that the value depends on the hardware), then the memory occupation gets capped at 3.4 Gb and test passes. For comparison, with pinned_mempool.free_all_blocks() memory occupation remains at the level around 2.4Gb. 

It seems to me, that there is some automatic garbage collection which can not cope with a rate that this test allocates/deallocates pinned memory. But works to at least some extent, if the rate is decreased by addition of sufficient sleeping time. Since I do not observe such problem with Numba on the same configuration, I guess that this bug is not in linux/python/cuda stack but rather in cupy itself.  



```
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp
import time

N = 10*1024*1024

cpu_data = np.zeros(N, dtype=np.float32)

mempool = cp.get_default_memory_pool()
pinned_mempool = cp.get_default_pinned_memory_pool()

for i in range(5000):
    gpu_data = cp.asarray(cpu_data)

    if i % 100 == 0:
        print(i, mempool.used_bytes(), mempool.total_bytes(), pinned_mempool.n_free_blocks())    

        time.sleep(0.1)
        #pinned_mempool.free_all_blocks()

print("Ok")

```

Description

Iteratively constructing an array via `xp.concatenate` appears to leak memory on a Jetson Orin Nano, running JetPack 5.1.3. (See the loop below). While the resident set size reported by `ps` remains below 1 MB, the GPU memory use reported in `/sys/kernel/debug/nvmap/iovmm/clients` climbs past 300 MB, eventually crashing the device if run for enough iterations.

### To Reproduce

The following loop causes GPU memory use by the Python process to exceed 300 MB:

```py
import time
import cupy as xp

array = xp.empty(0, dtype=xp.float64)
for i in range(1000):
    new_data = xp.random.rand(60)
    array = xp.concatenate([array, new_data])
    time.sleep(0.02)
```

In contrast, with pre-allocating the array, memory use is constant around 70 MB:

```py
import time
import cupy as xp

array = xp.empty(60000, dtype=xp.float64)
for i in range(1000):
    new_data = xp.random.rand(60)
    array[60*i:60*(i+1)] = new_data
    time.sleep(0.02)
```

Wheel (`pip install cupy-***`)

Description

Iteratively constructing an array via `xp.concatenate` appears to leak memory on a Jetson Orin Nano, running JetPack 5.1.3. (See the loop below). While the resident set size reported by `ps` remains below 1 MB, the GPU memory use reported in `/sys/kernel/debug/nvmap/iovmm/clients` climbs past 300 MB, eventually crashing the device if run for enough iterations.

### To Reproduce

The following loop causes GPU memory use by the Python process to exceed 300 MB:

```py
import time
import cupy as xp

array = xp.empty(0, dtype=xp.float64)
for i in range(1000):
    new_data = xp.random.rand(60)
    array = xp.concatenate([array, new_data])
    time.sleep(0.02)
```

In contrast, with pre-allocating the array, memory use is constant around 70 MB:

```py
import time
import cupy as xp

array = xp.empty(60000, dtype=xp.float64)
for i in range(1000):
    new_data = xp.random.rand(60)
    array[60*i:60*(i+1)] = new_data
    time.sleep(0.02)
```

### Installation

Wheel (`pip install cupy-***`)

Description

Iteratively constructing an array via `xp.concatenate` appears to leak memory on a Jetson Orin Nano, running JetPack 5.1.3. (See the loop below). While the resident set size reported by `ps` remains below 1 MB, the GPU memory use reported in `/sys/kernel/debug/nvmap/iovmm/clients` climbs past 300 MB, eventually crashing the device if run for enough iterations.

### To Reproduce

The following loop causes GPU memory use by the Python process to exceed 300 MB:

```py
import time
import cupy as xp

array = xp.empty(0, dtype=xp.float64)
for i in range(1000):
    new_data = xp.random.rand(60)
    array = xp.concatenate([array, new_data])
    time.sleep(0.02)
```

In contrast, with pre-allocating the array, memory use is constant around 70 MB:

```py
import time
import cupy as xp

array = xp.empty(60000, dtype=xp.float64)
for i in range(1000):
    new_data = xp.random.rand(60)
    array[60*i:60*(i+1)] = new_data
    time.sleep(0.02)
```

### Installation

Wheel (`pip install cupy-***`)

Are there plans to support the bfloat16 data type in the near future? This data type is becoming increasingly popular in LLM training. It looks like currently it's not supported. I.e., calling `y = cp.asarray(x)`, where `x` is a torch tensor of type `torch.bfloat16`, returns "TypeError: Got unsupported ScalarType BFloat16". Are there any recommended workarounds in the meantime?

For z of a few hundred this can see a speed gain over scipy's BVLS on the CPU; for a couple thousand, it can be a significant speed gain.

Description

In the scipy's implementation of svds we can get the number of singular values to be at max equal to min(M,N) using propack solver. I needed this particular implementation in the cupy's version of svds (where kmax is mandatorily lesser then min(M,N) )for a project that I am working in IIT Bombay's structure lab.

Can anyone guide me how to add this?

Check the scipy's implementation:

[Number of singular values and singular vectors to compute. Must satisfy 1 <= k <= kmax, where kmax=min(M, N) for solver='propack' and kmax=min(M, N) - 1 otherwise.](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.linalg.svds.html)

GPU version of `scipy.*` functions in `cupyx.scipy.*` namespace.

This is a tracker issue that summarizes the implementation status of each SciPy public module in CuPy. See the [comparison table](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/reference/comparison.html#scipy-cupy-apis) for details.

## Legends

* 🥚 Module not yet available in CuPy.
* 🐥 Module available in CuPy but coverage needs improvement.
* :shipit: Module available in CuPy and major features are implemented (may still have a few unimplemented APIs).
* ❌ Out of scope.

## List of Modules

- 🥚 Clustering package (`scipy.cluster`)
    - 🥚 K-means clustering and vector quantization (`scipy.cluster.vq`) (#5947)
    - 🥚 Hierarchical clustering (`scipy.cluster.hierarchy`) (#3434)
- 🥚 Constants (`scipy.constants`)
- :shipit: Discrete Fourier transforms (`scipy.fft`)
- :shipit: Legacy discrete Fourier transforms (`scipy.fftpack`) (note: deprecated, no further development planned)
- 🥚 Integration and ODEs (`scipy.integrate`) (#7019)
- :shipit: Interpolation (`scipy.interpolate`) (#7186)
- 🥚 Input and output (`scipy.io`)
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.arff`
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.matlab`
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.wavfile`
- 🐥 Linear algebra (`scipy.linalg`)
    - 🥚 Low-level BLAS functions (`scipy.linalg.blas`)
    - ❌ `scipy.linalg.cython_blas`
    - 🥚 Low-level LAPACK functions (`scipy.linalg.lapack`) c.f. [`cupyx.lapack`](https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/main/cupyx/lapack.py)
    - ❌ `scipy.linalg.cython_lapack`
    - 🥚 Interpolative matrix decomposition (`scipy.linalg.interpolative`)
- :shipit: Multidimensional image processing (`scipy.ndimage`)
- 🥚 Orthogonal distance regression (`scipy.odr`)
- 🥚 Optimization and root finding (`scipy.optimize`) (#6112)
- :shipit: Signal processing (`scipy.signal`) (#7403)
    - :shipit: `scipy.signal.windows` (#7404)
- :shipit: Sparse matrices (`scipy.sparse`)
    - :shipit: Sparse linear algebra (`scipy.sparse.linalg`)
    - 🐥 Compressed sparse graph routines (`scipy.sparse.csgraph`) (#2431)
- :shipit: Spatial algorithms and data structures (`scipy.spatial`) (#5946)
    - 🐥 Distance computations (`scipy.spatial.distance`) (#5946)
    - 🥚 Spatial transformations (`scipy.spatial.transform`)
- 🐥 Special functions (`scipy.special`) (note: planned to be backed by SciPy in future #8163)
- 🐥 Statistical functions (`scipy.stats`)
    - 🥚 Contingency table functions (`scipy.stats.contingency`) (note: RAFT could be used)
    - 🥚 `scipy.stats.distributions`
    - 🥚 Statistical functions for masked arrays (`scipy.stats.mstats`) (note: masked arrays unsupported in CuPy)
    - 🥚 Quasi-Monte Carlo submodule (`scipy.stats.qmc`)
    - 🥚 Random Number Generators (`scipy.stats.sampling`) (note: RAFT could be used)

**Note:** [Several modules in SciPy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/dev/api-dev/array_api.html#currently-supported-functionality) such as `scipy.cluster.hierarchy` accepts CuPy ndarrays as inputs through the Array API standard.

### Starter Task

If you are new to CuPy and wondering where to start, here are some good first things to try. They are relatively simple and independent.

* APIs under [Statistical Functions](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/reference/comparison.html#statistical-functions) (`scipy.stats`)
* `scipy.sparse.block_diag` (#7058)
* `scipy.sparse.load_npz`
* `scipy.sparse.save_npz`
* `scipy.constants.*` (hint: most things except for methods can just be borrowed from SciPy)

## Steps to Contribute

1. Fork and star :star: the CuPy repository :wink:

1. Pick a function you want to work on from any of the modules listed above. You can find the function in the [SciPy API Reference](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/index.html) to understand what should be implemented. If you want to work on new modules (🥚), first discuss with us on this issue.

1. Implement a function in your branch. If you need help, join [Gitter](https://gitter.im/cupy/community) or just ask for help in this issue.

1. Don't forget to write a test code!

1. Build CuPy and run tests to confirm that the function runs fine:
  `pip install -e . && pytest tests/cupyx_tests/scipy_tests/PATH_TO_YOUR_TEST`
   See the [Contribution Guide](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/contribution.html#unit-testing) for details.

1. Submit a pull-request to the `main` branch.

Note that you will need a GPU environment to develop CuPy.

edit: This PR adopts recent setuptools changes, specifically v74.0.0 (which [removed](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4600) `setuptools.msvc`) and v74.1.0+ (which [reverted](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4626) `setuptools.msvc` but requires explicit module import instead of `import setuptools`).

<details>
<summary>Original description</summary>

On Windows platform with setuptools 74+, it will now take 2-3 seconds to find `cl.exe`. This overhead happens only once per process, and only when the use of `nvcc` is requested.

`setuptools.msvc` (which we rely on for years and is now removed) was able to discover `cl.exe` very quickly as it directly reads the Windows registry. The new approach introduced in this PR (which only uses the public/documented setuptools API) retrives the compiler path through `vcvarsall.bat`, which incurs subprocess invocation.

In this PR, we add support for HMM/ATS memory systems so that users can opt-in and use `malloc` or `cudaMallocManaged` to allocate memory that is accessible to both CPU and GPU. This is a programming model feature allowing users of NVIDIA Grace Hopper systems to take full advantage of the coherent memory system.

This opt-in mechanism is currently guarded in a few steps, as outlined in both the doc change as well as test setup:
1. Set `CUPY_ENABLE_UMP=1`
2. Install `numpy_allocator`
   - note: I just found it's currently blocked on Python 3.12 ☹️ https://github.com/inaccel/numpy-allocator/issues/3
4. Set an allocator for both NumPy (CPU) and CuPy (GPU)

The net effect is we use NumPy and CuPy to represent CPU and GPU **execution** spaces, respectively, but the **memory** space is now unified, and memory transfer between CPU and GPU will become no-op if conditions are met. A proper stream synchronization is inserted wherever applicable, in order to ensure CPU/GPU do not have race condition.
In particular, the D2H copies are skipped by supporting the Python buffer protocol, which is generic enough for any host access not just NumPy.

Allocators for both NumPy and CuPy are needed because
- CuPy: we need a mechanism to 
   - allocate system memory (via `malloc`)
   - identify where the memory is from, quickly (via `mem.identity`)
- NumPy: we need to ensure allocated memory has right alignment for CuPy's kernels to consume, in order to avoid data corruption

Due to `numpy_allocator`'s requirement, we expose the memory allocation routines' symbols via `cdef public`, but with C instead of C++ linkage.","reactions":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/cupy/cupy/issues/comments/2373101458/reactions","total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"hooray":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"performed_via_github_app":null}}

+System allocated memory (SAM) support (**experimental!**)
+.........................................................
+
+It is possible to make both NumPy and CuPy use and share system allocated memory on Heterogeneous Memory Management
+(HMM) enabled systems or the NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchip. To activate this capability, currently you need to:
+
+1. Build CuPy from source and install `numpy_allocator <https://github.com/inaccel/numpy-allocator/>`_
+2. Set the environment variable ``CUPY_ENABLE_SAM=1``
+3. Make a memory pool for CuPy to draw system memory
+
+.. code-block:: py
+
+    import cupy as cp
+    cp.cuda.set_allocator(cp.cuda.MemoryPool(cp.cuda.memory.malloc_system).malloc)
+
+4. Switch to the aligned allocator for NumPy to draw system memory
+
+.. code-block:: py
+   
+    import cupy._core.numpy_allocator as ac
+    import numpy_allocator
+    import ctypes
+    lib = ctypes.CDLL(ac.__file__)
+    class my_allocator(metaclass=numpy_allocator.type):

+        _malloc_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._malloc)
+        _realloc_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._realloc)
+        _free_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._free)

+
+.. code-block:: py

+    rmm.mr.set_current_device_resource(mr)

+
+Currently on Grace Hopper, SAM can be migrated to the GPU, but is never migrated back to the host. If GPU memory is
+over-subscribed, this can cause other CUDA calls to fail with out-of-memory errors. To work around this problem, when
+using a system memory resource, you can reserve some GPU memory as headroom for other CUDA calls, and only conditionally
+set its preferred location to the GPU if the allocation would not eat into the headroom:

+    import rmm
+    headroom = 1 << 30  # 1 GiB
+    mr = rmm.mr.SamHeadroomMemoryResource(headroom=headroom)

{"action":"created","comment":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/cupy/cupy/pulls/comments/1774375604","pull_request_review_id":2326909205,"id":1774375604,"node_id":"PRRC_kwDOBFKgkM5pwtK0","diff_hunk":"@@ -198,3 +198,60 @@ Be sure to do this before any other CuPy operations.
 
    # Disable memory pool for pinned memory (CPU).
    cupy.cuda.set_pinned_memory_allocator(None)
+
+
+System allocated memory (SAM) support (**experimental!**)
+.........................................................
+
+It is possible to make both NumPy and CuPy use and share system allocated memory on Heterogeneous Memory Management
+(HMM) enabled systems or the NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchip. To activate this capability, currently you need to:
+
+1. Build CuPy from source and install `numpy_allocator <https://github.com/inaccel/numpy-allocator/>`_
+2. Set the environment variable ``CUPY_ENABLE_SAM=1``
+3. Make a memory pool for CuPy to draw system memory
+
+.. code-block:: py
+
+    import cupy as cp
+    cp.cuda.set_allocator(cp.cuda.MemoryPool(cp.cuda.memory.malloc_system).malloc)
+
+4. Switch to the aligned allocator for NumPy to draw system memory
+
+.. code-block:: py
+   
+    import cupy._core.numpy_allocator as ac
+    import numpy_allocator
+    import ctypes
+    lib = ctypes.CDLL(ac.__file__)
+    class my_allocator(metaclass=numpy_allocator.type):
+        _calloc_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._calloc)
+        _malloc_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._malloc)
+        _realloc_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._realloc)
+        _free_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._free)
+    my_allocator.__enter__()  # change the allocator globally
+
+For CuPy, alternatively you can use the CuPy allocator from RAPIDS Memory Manager (RMM):
+
+.. code-block:: py
+
+    import cupy as cp
+    import rmm
+    mr = rmm.mr.SystemMemoryResource()
+    rmm.mr.set_current_device_resource(mr)
+    cp.cuda.set_allocator(rmm.allocators.cupy.rmm_cupy_allocator)
+
+Currently on Grace Hopper, SAM can be migrated to the GPU, but is never migrated back to the host. If GPU memory is
+over-subscribed, this can cause other CUDA calls to fail with out-of-memory errors. To work around this problem, when
+using a system memory resource, you can reserve some GPU memory as headroom for other CUDA calls, and only conditionally
+set its preferred location to the GPU if the allocation would not eat into the headroom:
+
+.. code-block:: py
+

+System allocated memory (SAM) support (**experimental!**)
+.........................................................
+
+It is possible to make both NumPy and CuPy use and share system allocated memory on Heterogeneous Memory Management
+(HMM) enabled systems or the NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchip. To activate this capability, currently you need to:
+
+1. Build CuPy from source and install `numpy_allocator <https://github.com/inaccel/numpy-allocator/>`_
+2. Set the environment variable ``CUPY_ENABLE_SAM=1``
+3. Make a memory pool for CuPy to draw system memory
+
+.. code-block:: py
+
+    import cupy as cp
+    cp.cuda.set_allocator(cp.cuda.MemoryPool(cp.cuda.memory.malloc_system).malloc)
+
+4. Switch to the aligned allocator for NumPy to draw system memory
+
+.. code-block:: py
+   
+    import cupy._core.numpy_allocator as ac
+    import numpy_allocator
+    import ctypes
+    lib = ctypes.CDLL(ac.__file__)
+    class my_allocator(metaclass=numpy_allocator.type):
+        _calloc_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._calloc)
+        _malloc_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._malloc)
+        _realloc_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._realloc)
+        _free_ = ctypes.addressof(lib._free)
+    my_allocator.__enter__()  # change the allocator globally
+
+For CuPy, alternatively you can use the CuPy allocator from RAPIDS Memory Manager (RMM):
+
+.. code-block:: py
+
+    import cupy as cp
+    import rmm
+    mr = rmm.mr.SystemMemoryResource()
+    rmm.mr.set_current_device_resource(mr)

# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built

I tried to compile cupy with the rocm libraries that Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS provides in its default package sources. This did not work because the cupy build tool chain was not able to find hipblas. Listed below are all the files that are installed with `libhipblas-dev` and `libhipblas0`. I tested both, not setting `ROCM_HOME` at all and setting it to `/usr`. In both cases cupy could not find hipblas.

```

I tried to compile cupy with the rocm libraries that Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS provides in its default package sources. This did not work because the cupy build tool chain was not able to find hipblas. Listed below are all the files that are installed with `libhipblas-dev` and `libhipblas0`. I tested both, not setting `ROCM_HOME` at all and setting it to `/usr`. In both cases cupy could not find hipblas.

Added [CUDA Graphs conditional nodes](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/dynamic-control-flow-in-cuda-graphs-with-conditional-nodes/) support for CuPy with the _functional_ API.

CUDA Graphs conditional nodes can be used in CUDA 12.4+ and this feature adds data-dependent dynamic control flow such as while-like loop or if-like branch conditions into CUDA Graphs.

In summary, this PR includes the following changes:

1. Support for some low-level CUDA runtime API to use conditional nodes from CuPy.
2. Functional API to define CUDA Graph with conditional nodes

From my personal experience of over ten years maintaining several Python libraries, I can say that while making APIs public is easy, it is often irreversible and can lead to constant challenges for the maintainers, affecting the velocity of the development. Even clearly labelling APIs as "private" (or "undocumented"), it can still make for a tough decision to change or remove it, and once it's done, we inevitably receive a barrage of bug reports claiming the library is broken. Actually it took us years to remove the `compile_with_cache` (#5297) or private namespaces (#3420).

Once again, to clear up any possible misunderstanding, your request is completely understandable and legitimate. In fact, I was the one who submitted https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/79 when I was merely an early user of CuPy.

I've cross-liked this PR in #130 to collect and track the needs for the Cython-level APIs. When it comes to exposing a public Cython API, I believe we will need:

1. A clear distinction between public and private APIs. This might require some refactoring.
2. Documentation to communicate users about the compatibility level they can expect from the Cython API, like SciPy does.
3. Continuous integration to test the Cython API. As of now, we can't determine whether or not the Cython cimport dependencies are closed within the PXD files you've added in this pull request.

As we see it, these are our responsibilities in providing a stable product to our users and keeping the project maintainable.","reactions":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/cupy/cupy/issues/comments/2362684089/reactions","total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"hooray":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"performed_via_github_app":null}}

> I also tried another nvidia package `cunumeric` and it didn't support windows and was not going to.

> CuPy bindings are `cdef`d, this is why `pxd` exports needed.

CuPy bindings are `cdef`d, this is why `pxd` exports needed. Bubbling up from native calls and derouting over python makes the whole process noticeably slower (I'd say ~2x), it is not negligible.

GPU version of `scipy.*` functions in `cupyx.scipy.*` namespace.

This is a tracker issue that summarizes the implementation status of each SciPy public module in CuPy. See the [comparison table](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/reference/comparison.html#scipy-cupy-apis) for details.

## Legends

* 🥚 Module not yet available in CuPy.
* 🐥 Module available in CuPy but coverage needs improvement.
* :shipit: Module available in CuPy and major features are implemented (may still have a few unimplemented APIs).
* ❌ Out of scope.

## List of Modules

- 🥚 Clustering package (`scipy.cluster`)
    - 🥚 K-means clustering and vector quantization (`scipy.cluster.vq`) (#5947)
    - 🥚 Hierarchical clustering (`scipy.cluster.hierarchy`) (#3434)
- 🥚 Constants (`scipy.constants`)
- :shipit: Discrete Fourier transforms (`scipy.fft`)
- :shipit: Legacy discrete Fourier transforms (`scipy.fftpack`) (note: deprecated, no further development planned)
- 🥚 Integration and ODEs (`scipy.integrate`) (#7019)
- :shipit: Interpolation (`scipy.interpolate`) (#7186)
- 🥚 Input and output (`scipy.io`)
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.arff`
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.matlab`
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.wavfile`
- 🐥 Linear algebra (`scipy.linalg`)
    - 🥚 Low-level BLAS functions (`scipy.linalg.blas`)
    - ❌ `scipy.linalg.cython_blas`
    - 🥚 Low-level LAPACK functions (`scipy.linalg.lapack`) c.f. [`cupyx.lapack`](https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/main/cupyx/lapack.py)
    - ❌ `scipy.linalg.cython_lapack`
    - 🥚 Interpolative matrix decomposition (`scipy.linalg.interpolative`)
- :shipit: Multidimensional image processing (`scipy.ndimage`)
- 🥚 Orthogonal distance regression (`scipy.odr`)
- 🥚 Optimization and root finding (`scipy.optimize`) (#6112)
- :shipit: Signal processing (`scipy.signal`) (#7403)
    - :shipit: `scipy.signal.windows` (#7404)
- :shipit: Sparse matrices (`scipy.sparse`)
    - :shipit: Sparse linear algebra (`scipy.sparse.linalg`)
    - 🐥 Compressed sparse graph routines (`scipy.sparse.csgraph`) (#2431)
- :shipit: Spatial algorithms and data structures (`scipy.spatial`) (#5946)
    - 🐥 Distance computations (`scipy.spatial.distance`) (#5946)
    - 🥚 Spatial transformations (`scipy.spatial.transform`)
- 🐥 Special functions (`scipy.special`) (note: planned to be backed by SciPy in future #8163)
- 🐥 Statistical functions (`scipy.stats`)
    - 🥚 Contingency table functions (`scipy.stats.contingency`) (note: RAFT could be used)
    - 🥚 `scipy.stats.distributions`
    - 🥚 Statistical functions for masked arrays (`scipy.stats.mstats`) (note: masked arrays unsupported in CuPy)
    - 🥚 Quasi-Monte Carlo submodule (`scipy.stats.qmc`)
    - 🥚 Random Number Generators (`scipy.stats.sampling`) (note: RAFT could be used)

**Note:** [Several modules in SciPy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/dev/api-dev/array_api.html#currently-supported-functionality) such as `scipy.cluster.hierarchy` accepts CuPy ndarrays as inputs through the Array API standard.

### Starter Task

If you are new to CuPy and wondering where to start, here are some good first things to try. They are relatively simple and independent.

* APIs under [Statistical Functions](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/reference/comparison.html#statistical-functions) (`scipy.stats`)
* `scipy.sparse.block_diag` (#7058)
* `scipy.sparse.load_npz`
* `scipy.sparse.save_npz`
* `scipy.constants.*` (hint: most things except for methods can just be borrowed from SciPy)

## Steps to Contribute

1. Fork and star :star: the CuPy repository :wink:

1. Pick a function you want to work on from any of the modules listed above. You can find the function in the [SciPy API Reference](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/index.html) to understand what should be implemented. If you want to work on new modules (🥚), first discuss with us on this issue.

1. Implement a function in your branch. If you need help, join [Gitter](https://gitter.im/cupy/community) or just ask for help in this issue.

1. Don't forget to write a test code!

1. Build CuPy and run tests to confirm that the function runs fine:
  `pip install -e . && pytest tests/cupyx_tests/scipy_tests/PATH_TO_YOUR_TEST`
   See the [Contribution Guide](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/contribution.html#unit-testing) for details.

1. Submit a pull-request to the `main` branch.

Note that you will need a GPU environment to develop CuPy.

Description

Firstly, building CuPy on ROCm requires additional CFLAGS:
```
export CFLAGS="-I/opt/rocm/include/hipblas -I/opt/rocm/include/hipsparse -I/opt/rocm/include/hipfft -I/opt/rocm/include/rocsolver -I/opt/rocm/include/rccl"
```
But `pip install cupy` still fails after several minutes:
```
error: Command "x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc -Wno-unused-result -Wsign-compare -DNDEBUG -g -fwrapv -O2 -Wall -g -fstack-protector-strong -Wformat -Werror=format-security -g -fwrapv -O2 -I/opt/rocm/include/hipblas -I/opt/rocm/include/hipsparse -I/opt/rocm/include/hipfft -I/opt/rocm/include/rocsolver -I/opt/rocm/include/rccl -Wdate-time -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -fPIC -D_FORCE_INLINES=1 -DCUPY_USE_HIP=1 -D__HIP_PLATFORM_AMD__=1 -D__HIP_PLATFORM_HCC__=1 -DCUPY_CACHE_KEY=d4770f4cb60796d63570de639682672dffe05289 -DCUPY_CUB_VERSION_CODE=300000 -I/opt/rocm/hipfft/include -I/opt/rocm/include/hipcub -I/tmp/pip-install-0x7cot68/cupy_f9bce70497514fa68cfe3560b85351d4/cupy/_core/include -I/opt/rocm/include -I/opt/rocm/include/hip -I/opt/rocm/include/rocrand -I/opt/rocm/include/hiprand -I/opt/rocm/include/roctracer -I/usr/include/python3.10 -c cupy_backends/cuda/api/runtime.cpp -o build/temp.linux-x86_64-3.10/cupy_backends/cuda/api/runtime.o -std=c++11" failed with exit status 1
```
(It's strange that `cupy_backends/cuda/api/runtime.cpp` is compiled with `x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc`)

### To Reproduce

```bash
export CFLAGS="-I/opt/rocm/include/hipblas -I/opt/rocm/include/hipsparse -I/opt/rocm/include/hipfft -I/opt/rocm/include/rocsolver"
export CUPY_INSTALL_USE_HIP=1
export ROCM_HOME=/opt/rocm
export HCC_AMDGPU_TARGET=gfx906
sudo -E pip3 install cupy
```

### Installation

Source (`pip install cupy`)

Not available

Description

Pinned memory created with `cupyx.empty_pinned(...)`, `cupyx.zeros_pinned(...)`, et cetera, is not released by Python garbage collection, even when the relevant Python objects should be out of scope. The memory is not released until the Python process exits.

### To Reproduce

```python3
import numpy as np
import cupyx
import gc
input("Allocating pinned memory with cupyx...")
a = cupyx.zeros_pinned(2000000000, dtype=np.float32)
input("Check the RAM usage, particularly 'shared memory' in htop, then press Enter to remove the array from scope.")
del a
input("The array has been removed from scope. Check the memory usage again. The pinned memory has not been released. Press enter to explicitly run the Python garbage collection.")
gc.collect()
input("Garbage collection has been called explicitly. Check the memory usage again. It hasn't changed. Press Enter to quit. Memory will be released when the Python process exits.")
```

After looking into `gemm`, it seems that the current code relies on `flags.c_contiguous` and `flags.f_contiguous` to determine whether a copy is necessary. However, an array with a stride of 1 itemsize in any dimension can be handled directly by cublas.
For example
```
cp.empty(5, 4)
```
will create a c-contiguous array with strides (80, 8), but:
```
cp.empty(5, 4)[:, :3]
```
is neither c nor f contiguous, despite having the same stride as the array above.
The BLAS routines have a concept of stride which is different from the shape. As long as one of the stride is 1, BLAS does not require a copy.

For a multiplication of a 10,000 x 10,000 matrix by a 10,000 vector, the cost is 5x vs using `gemv` and avoiding the copy. This ratio increases with the size of the matrices. For 1,000 x 1,000 matrices, it is 2x. For 100 x 100 matrices, it is 15%.

### Additional Information

Example: 

```python
import cupy
import cupyx

# Coo Matrix
data  = cupy.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1], 'f')
row  = cupy.array([0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], 'i')
col   = cupy.array([0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2], 'i')

A     = cupyx.scipy.sparse.coo_matrix((data, (row, col)), shape=(3, 3),dtype=cupy.float32 )
B     = cupyx.scipy.sparse.csr_matrix((data, (row, col)), shape=(3, 3) ,dtype=cupy.float32)
C     = cupyx.scipy.sparse.csc_matrix((data, (row, col)), shape=(3, 3) ,dtype=cupy.float32)

squared_diff = cp.ElementwiseKernel(
   'float32 x, float32 y',
   'float32 z',
   'z = (x - y) * (x - y)',
   'squared_diff')

# Elementwise Kernel for Sparse Matrices.
# Same for A,A ; B,B; C,C
squared_diff(C,C)
# (C-C)*(C-C) works work.

Description

While trying to use `cp.linalg.eigh` on a batch of matrices, there was some specific size beyond which I would get an error `CUSOLVERError: CUSOLVER_STATUS_INVALID_VALUE`

I tried to debug and it came down to `_cusolver.cheevjBatched_bufferSize`, but the cuda error isn't very helpful since the parameters all seem fine except for the size of the input.

### To Reproduce

here i'm trying to get the buffer size for a batch of (4, 4) matrices

```py
from cupy_backends.cuda.libs import cusolver as _cusolver
from cupy.cuda import device as _device
from cupy_backends.cuda.libs import cublas as _cublas
import cupy as _cupy
import numpy as _numpy

def test_size(s, mat_size=(4, 4)):
    # Mostly copied from
    # https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/v11.4.0/cupy/cusolver.pyx#L569

    a = np.zeros( (s, *mat_size), dtype=np.complex64)

    dtype, v_dtype = _cupy.linalg._util.linalg_common_type(a, reject_float16=False)
    real_dtype = dtype.char.lower()
    w_dtype = v_dtype.char.lower()

    *batch_shape, m, lda = a.shape
    batch_size = _numpy.prod(batch_shape)

    a = a.reshape(batch_size, m, lda)
    vp = _cupy.array(a.swapaxes(-2, -1), order='C', copy=True, dtype=dtype)

    jobz = _cusolver.CUSOLVER_EIG_MODE_VECTOR
    uplo = _cublas.CUBLAS_FILL_MODE_LOWER

    w = _cupy.empty((batch_size, m), real_dtype).swapaxes(-2, -1)

    dev_info = _cupy.empty((batch_size,), _cupy.int32)
    handle = _device.Device().cusolver_handle
    params = _cusolver.createSyevjInfo()

    print(f"{handle = }, {jobz = }, {uplo = }")
    print(f"{vp.size = }, {vp.data.ptr = }")
    print(f"{w.size = }, {w.data.ptr = }")
    print(f"{params = }")
    print(f"{batch_size = }")


    work_size = _cusolver.cheevjBatched_bufferSize(handle, jobz, uplo, m, vp.data.ptr, lda, w.data.ptr, params, batch_size)
  

    print("---------------")
    print(f"{work_size = }")
    return work_size

```

In numpy, you can use `==` and `!=` to check which item in an `ndarray` is None.
In cupy, comparing an array to None raises `NotImplemented`.

Numpy example:
```
import numpy as np
>>> a = np.array([1, 2, None])
>>> a == None
array([False, False,  True])
```

Cupy example:
```
import cupy
>>> a = cupy.array([1, 2, cupy.nan])
>>> a == None
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "cupy/_core/core.pyx", line 1217, in cupy._core.core._ndarray_base.__richcmp__
TypeError: operand type(s) all returned NotImplemented from __array_ufunc__(<ufunc 'equal'>, '__call__', array([ 1.,  2., nan]), None): 'ndarray', 'NoneType'
```

Notice that numpy checks equality against `None` and not against `np.nan`

In numpy, you can use `==` and `!=` to check which item in an `ndarray` is None.
In cupy, comparing an array to None raises `NotImplemented`.

Numpy example:
```
import numpy as np
>>> a = np.array([1, 2, None])
>>> a == None
array([False, False,  True])
```

Cupy example:
```
import cupy
>>> a = cupy.array([1, 2, cupy.nan])
>>> a == None
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "cupy/_core/core.pyx", line 1217, in cupy._core.core._ndarray_base.__richcmp__
TypeError: operand type(s) all returned NotImplemented from __array_ufunc__(<ufunc 'equal'>, '__call__', array([ 1.,  2., nan]), None): 'ndarray', 'NoneType'
```

Notice that numpy checks equality against `None` and not against `np.nan`

                    dvs=dvs_mode,
                    layer=j,
                )

        setattr(self, f"block", blocks)

        elif isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm2d):
            nn.init.constant_(m.bias, 0)
            nn.init.constant_(m.weight, 1.0)

        block = getattr(self, f"block")
        patch_embed = getattr(self, f"patch_embed")

        x, _, hook = patch_embed(x, hook=hook)
        for blk in block:
            x, _, hook = blk(x, hook=hook)

        x = x.flatten(3).mean(3)
        return x, hook

        if hook is not None:
            hook["head_lif"] = x.detach()

        x = self.head(x)
        if not self.TET:

        setattr(self, f"block", blocks)

        # classification head
        if spike_mode in ["lif", "alif", "blif"]:
            self.head_lif = MultiStepLIFNode(tau=2.0, detach_reset=True, backend="cupy")
        elif spike_mode == "plif":
            self.head_lif = MultiStepParametricLIFNode(
                init_tau=2.0, detach_reset=True, backend="cupy"
            )
        self.head = (
            nn.Linear(embed_dims, num_classes) if num_classes > 0 else nn.Identity()
        )
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    def _init_weights(self, m):
        if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d):
            trunc_normal_(m.weight, std=0.02)
            if m.bias is not None:
                nn.init.constant_(m.bias, 0)
        elif isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm2d):
            nn.init.constant_(m.bias, 0)
            nn.init.constant_(m.weight, 1.0)

    def forward_features(self, x, hook=None):
        block = getattr(self, f"block")
        patch_embed = getattr(self, f"patch_embed")

        x, _, hook = patch_embed(x, hook=hook)
        for blk in block:
            x, _, hook = blk(x, hook=hook)

        x = x.flatten(3).mean(3)
        return x, hook

    def forward(self, x, hook=None):
        if len(x.shape) < 5:
            x = (x.unsqueeze(0)).repeat(self.T, 1, 1, 1, 1)
        else:
            x = x.transpose(0, 1).contiguous()

        x, hook = self.forward_features(x, hook=hook)
        x = self.head_lif(x)
        if hook is not None:
            hook["head_lif"] = x.detach()

        x = self.head(x)
        if not self.TET:
            x = x.mean(0)
        return x, hook


@register_model
def sdt(**kwargs):
    model = SpikeDrivenTransformer(
        **kwargs,
    )
    model.default_cfg = _cfg()
    return model

# 创建模型实例

# 打印模型

Description

I have an example of a function that returns two arrays of shape `[2, 2, 2]` and `[2, 2]`. When I apply `cupy.fuse` to this function and run it, the returned arrays are both shaped `[2, 2, 2]` with the second return broadcasted to match the first returned array. This is not correct.
I expect the `cupy.fuse`'d function to either return the correct size arrays, or error out if this is not supported.

### To Reproduce

```py
import cupy as cp

@cp.fuse
def foo(a, b):
  return 2.0*a, 3.0*b

a = cp.ones([2, 2, 2])
b = cp.ones([2, 2])

r1, r2 = foo(a, b)
print(f"r1.shape = {r1.shape}\n r1 = {r1}")
print(f"r2.shape = {r2.shape}\n r2 = {r2}")
```
Running this, you will get:
```
r1.shape = (2, 2, 2)

  [2. 2.]]

  [2. 2.]]]
r2.shape = (2, 2, 2)

  [3. 3.]]

  [3. 3.]]]
```

When trying to show config or running the example below, Cupy fails to find `libnvrtc`:
```
RuntimeError: CuPy failed to load libnvrtc.so.12: OSError: libnvrtc.so.12: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
```

This was never an issue until v13 (worked in previous versions).

**Problem**

I am getting a compilation error when compiling CUDA code with cupy and CUDA 11.8 since a new version of the visual studio compiler has been released (17.0)
the error is 
```
C:\Miniconda\envs\cupy_project\include\crt/host_config.h(153): fatal error C1189: #error:  -- unsupported Microsoft Visual Studio version! Use at your own risk.
 E               nvcc warning : The -std=c++11 flag is not supported with the configured host compiler. Flag will be ignored.
```
The problem is discussed on the NVidida form [here](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/problems-with-latest-vs2022-update/294150/2)

**Solution**

As a mitigation we could add the flag `allow-unsupported-compiler` in the function [compile_using_nvcc`](https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/aa9b743d07eacbfc7d715369b762879c3c362d9e/cupy/cuda/compiler.py#L341)

```py
# Write the code here
```

create a pyhon conda environment using the environment file 
```
name:  runtime
channels:
  - defaults

dependencies:

pip install cupy-cuda11x==12.3.0
```

Description

The dtype of returned indices in `cupy.unique(..., return_index=True, return_inverse=True)` appear to be always `int64`, even if the input array is `int32` and its size is within the range of `int32` limit.
Example below, where `grains` would be an `int32` array of grain labels in a flattened image of size 8192**2:
```
unic, iunic, iback = cp.unique(grains, return_index=True, return_inverse=True)
```
I would expect the dtype of `iunic` and `iback` here to remain `int32`, while they are returned as `int64`.
This leads to a `OutOfMemoryError` when dealing with (even moderately) large arrays.
Would if be possible to add a `dtype` parameter in the `cupy.unique()` function ? 

Now, there is another problem with the ability to flush (afterwards) the memory that was cached during the internal business of the `cp.unique()` function. Not sure if this is a bug or if this is due to my limited understanding of cupy.    
Namely, after a call to `mempool.free_all_blocks()` following the above `cp.unique()` operation, there is still a lot of remaining `free_bytes` on top of the `used_bytes` corresponding to the input and returned arrays.
Complete test example here:

```
import cupy as cp
DTYPEi = cp.int32
mempool = cp.get_default_memory_pool()

ngrains = 64
npix = 1024**2
grains = cp.repeat(cp.arange(ngrains, dtype=DTYPEi), npix)
cp.random.shuffle(grains)

mempool.free_all_blocks()
print(mempool.used_bytes()/1024**2, mempool.total_bytes()/1024**2, mempool.free_bytes()/1024**2)
# returns "256.0 256.0 0.0"

unic, iunic, iback = cp.unique(grains, return_index=True, return_inverse=True)
print(iback.dtype)
# returns "int64", I would expect it to remain "int32"
print(mempool.used_bytes()/1024**2, mempool.total_bytes()/1024**2, mempool.free_bytes()/1024**2)
# returns "768.0009765625 3095.27783203125 2327.27685546875"

mempool.free_all_blocks()
print(mempool.used_bytes()/1024**2, mempool.total_bytes()/1024**2, mempool.free_bytes()/1024**2)
# returns "768.0009765625 1559.27783203125 791.27685546875"
```
So, there are still 791 MiB cached somewhere in GPU the memory on top of the ~768 MiB of the input and returned arrays.
I would have expected the call to `free_all_blocks()` to get rid of it...

GPU version of `scipy.*` functions in `cupyx.scipy.*` namespace.

This is a tracker issue that summarizes the implementation status of each SciPy public module in CuPy. See the [comparison table](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/reference/comparison.html#scipy-cupy-apis) for details.

## Legends

* 🥚 Module not yet available in CuPy.
* 🐥 Module available in CuPy but coverage needs improvement.
* :shipit: Module available in CuPy and major features are implemented (may still have a few unimplemented APIs).
* ❌ Out of scope.

## List of Modules

- 🥚 Clustering package (`scipy.cluster`)
    - 🥚 K-means clustering and vector quantization (`scipy.cluster.vq`) (#5947)
    - 🥚 Hierarchical clustering (`scipy.cluster.hierarchy`) (#3434)
- 🥚 Constants (`scipy.constants`)
- :shipit: Discrete Fourier transforms (`scipy.fft`)
- :shipit: Legacy discrete Fourier transforms (`scipy.fftpack`) (note: deprecated, no further development planned)
- 🥚 Integration and ODEs (`scipy.integrate`) (#7019)
- :shipit: Interpolation (`scipy.interpolate`) (#7186)
- 🥚 Input and output (`scipy.io`)
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.arff`
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.matlab`
    - 🥚 `scipy.io.wavfile`
- 🐥 Linear algebra (`scipy.linalg`)
    - 🥚 Low-level BLAS functions (`scipy.linalg.blas`)
    - ❌ `scipy.linalg.cython_blas`
    - 🥚 Low-level LAPACK functions (`scipy.linalg.lapack`) c.f. [`cupyx.lapack`](https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/main/cupyx/lapack.py)
    - ❌ `scipy.linalg.cython_lapack`
    - 🥚 Interpolative matrix decomposition (`scipy.linalg.interpolative`)
- :shipit: Multidimensional image processing (`scipy.ndimage`)
- 🥚 Orthogonal distance regression (`scipy.odr`)
- 🥚 Optimization and root finding (`scipy.optimize`) (#6112)
- :shipit: Signal processing (`scipy.signal`) (#7403)
    - :shipit: `scipy.signal.windows` (#7404)
- :shipit: Sparse matrices (`scipy.sparse`)
    - :shipit: Sparse linear algebra (`scipy.sparse.linalg`)
    - 🐥 Compressed sparse graph routines (`scipy.sparse.csgraph`) (#2431)
- :shipit: Spatial algorithms and data structures (`scipy.spatial`) (#5946)
    - 🐥 Distance computations (`scipy.spatial.distance`) (#5946)
    - 🥚 Spatial transformations (`scipy.spatial.transform`)
- 🐥 Special functions (`scipy.special`) (note: planned to be backed by SciPy in future #8163)
- 🐥 Statistical functions (`scipy.stats`)
    - 🥚 Contingency table functions (`scipy.stats.contingency`) (note: RAFT could be used)
    - 🥚 `scipy.stats.distributions`
    - 🥚 Statistical functions for masked arrays (`scipy.stats.mstats`) (note: masked arrays unsupported in CuPy)
    - 🥚 Quasi-Monte Carlo submodule (`scipy.stats.qmc`)
    - 🥚 Random Number Generators (`scipy.stats.sampling`) (note: RAFT could be used)

**Note:** [Several modules in SciPy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/dev/api-dev/array_api.html#currently-supported-functionality) such as `scipy.cluster.hierarchy` accepts CuPy ndarrays as inputs through the Array API standard.

### Starter Task

If you are new to CuPy and wondering where to start, here are some good first things to try. They are relatively simple and independent.

* APIs under [Statistical Functions](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/reference/comparison.html#statistical-functions) (`scipy.stats`)
* `scipy.sparse.block_diag` (#7058)
* `scipy.sparse.load_npz`
* `scipy.sparse.save_npz`
* `scipy.constants.*` (hint: most things except for methods can just be borrowed from SciPy)

## Steps to Contribute

1. Fork and star :star: the CuPy repository :wink:

1. Pick a function you want to work on from any of the modules listed above. You can find the function in the [SciPy API Reference](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/index.html) to understand what should be implemented. If you want to work on new modules (🥚), first discuss with us on this issue.

1. Implement a function in your branch. If you need help, join [Gitter](https://gitter.im/cupy/community) or just ask for help in this issue.

1. Don't forget to write a test code!

1. Build CuPy and run tests to confirm that the function runs fine:
  `pip install -e . && pytest tests/cupyx_tests/scipy_tests/PATH_TO_YOUR_TEST`
   See the [Contribution Guide](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/contribution.html#unit-testing) for details.

1. Submit a pull-request to the `main` branch.

Note that you will need a GPU environment to develop CuPy.

I tried to use linalg inv for a batch of small random matrices with streams. I observed the error that the outputs are filled with NANs and infs. 

In the code snipped, the inverse of the identity matrix is taken. In the first call, the output is correct, but not in the second call.
When rng is commented out the error does not occur. In addition, the error does not occur with additional device synchronization.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/86b5ce82-f7db-402a-95d6-0c6332bde686)

### To Reproduce

```py
import cupy as cp

def test_inv_stream(
    matrix_size,
    batch_size,
    dtype
):
    rng = cp.random.default_rng(seed=1)

    a_d = cp.empty((batch_size, matrix_size, matrix_size), dtype=dtype)

    # increase numerical stability
    for i in range(batch_size):
        a_d[i] = cp.eye(matrix_size, dtype=dtype)

    stream1 = cp.cuda.stream.Stream(non_blocking=True)
    
    stream1.synchronize()
    with stream1:
        inv_ref_d = cp.linalg.inv(a_d)
    stream1.synchronize()
    print(inv_ref_d)

test_inv_stream(5, 1, cp.float64)
test_inv_stream(10, 1, cp.float64)
```

Wheel (`pip install cupy-***`)

When I'm using `cupyx.scipy.linalg.expm` on a 2x2 complex matrix, there is a small (~3e-6) absolute error wrt the correct value and wrt `scipy.linalg.expm`.



### To Reproduce

```py
from scipy.linalg import expm
import cupy as cp
from cupyx.scipy.linalg import expm as cuexpm
import numpy as np


def test_expm(theta):
    dtype = "complex128"
    X = np.rot90(np.eye(2)).astype(dtype)
    eP1 = np.eye(2) * np.cos(theta) + 1j * X * np.sin(theta)
    eP2 = expm(1j * theta * X)
    eP3 = cuexpm(1j * theta * cp.asarray(X)).get()
    assert np.allclose(eP1, eP2, atol=1e-10)
    assert np.allclose(eP1, eP3, atol=1e-10) # fails here


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for v in [0.2, np.pi, 2 * np.pi, 3 * np.pi, np.pi / 2, np.pi / 4]:
        try:
            test_expm(v)
            print(f"v Test for theta={v} passed")
        except AssertionError:
            print(f"x Test for theta={v} failed")
```

x Test for theta=1.5707963267948966 failed
v Test for theta=0.7853981633974483 passed
```

I tried to use linalg inv for a batch of small random matrices with streams. I observed the error that the outputs are filled with NANs and infs. 

In the code snipped, the inverse of the identity matrix is taken. In the first call, the output is correct, but not in the second call.
When rng is commented out the error does not occur. In addition, the error does not occur with additional device synchronization.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/86b5ce82-f7db-402a-95d6-0c6332bde686)

### To Reproduce

```py
import cupy as cp

def test_inv_stream(
    matrix_size,
    batch_size,
    dtype
):
    rng = cp.random.default_rng(seed=1)

    a_d = cp.empty((batch_size, matrix_size, matrix_size), dtype=dtype)

    # increase numerical stability
    for i in range(batch_size):
        a_d[i] = cp.eye(matrix_size, dtype=dtype)

    stream1 = cp.cuda.stream.Stream(non_blocking=True)
    
    stream1.synchronize()
    with stream1:
        inv_ref_d = cp.linalg.inv(a_d)
    stream1.synchronize()
    print(inv_ref_d)

test_inv_stream(5, 1, cp.float64)
test_inv_stream(10, 1, cp.float64)
```

When I'm using `cupyx.scipy.linalg.expm` on a 2x2 complex matrix, there is a small (~3e-6) absolute error wrt the correct value and wrt `scipy.linalg.expm`.



### To Reproduce

```py
from scipy.linalg import expm
import cupy as cp
from cupyx.scipy.linalg import expm as cuexpm
import numpy as np


def test_expm(theta):
    dtype = "complex128"
    X = np.rot90(np.eye(2)).astype(dtype)
    eP1 = np.eye(2) * np.cos(theta) + 1j * X * np.sin(theta)
    eP2 = expm(1j * theta * X)
    eP3 = cuexpm(1j * theta * cp.asarray(X)).get()
    assert np.allclose(eP1, eP2, atol=1e-10)
    assert np.allclose(eP1, eP3, atol=1e-10)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for v in [0.2, np.pi, 2 * np.pi, 3 * np.pi, np.pi / 2, np.pi / 4]:
        try:
            test_expm(v)
            print(f"v Test for theta={v} passed")
        except AssertionError:
            print(f"x Test for theta={v} failed")
```

Description

While using `cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu`, I noticed that subsequent `solve()` steps using the `SuperLU` result returned from `cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu` are a lot slower (~120x slower in the example below) than the equivalent `scipy` operation on the CPU. 

### To Reproduce

Here's the `scipy` version (note I'm using the ipython/jupyter `%time` magic for timing the `linalg.splu` and `.solve` lines):

```py
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import random, csc_matrix
from scipy.sparse import linalg

size = 10_000
A = random(size, size, density=0.5, random_state=2)
A = csc_matrix(A)
x = np.random.default_rng(seed=2).random(size)
%time B = linalg.splu(A)    # 1min 10s
%time result = B.solve(x)   # 81.5 ms
```

The output here gives a runtime of 1min 10s for the `B = linalg.splu(A)` line and 81.5 ms for the `result = B.solve(x)` line.

Switching to the equivalent `cupy` version:

```python
import cupy as cp
from cupyx.scipy.sparse import random, csc_matrix
from cupyx.scipy.sparse import linalg

size = 10_000
A = random(size, size, density=0.5, random_state=2)
A = csc_matrix(A)
x = cp.random.default_rng(seed=2).random(size)
%time B = linalg.splu(A)    # 1min 15s
%time result = B.solve(x)   # 9.86 s
```

In this case, the `B = linalg.splu(A)` line takes ~1min 15s , which is similar to the `scipy` CPU version. This is expected as the docs https://docs.cupy.dev/en/stable/reference/generated/cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu.html say that this step actually just happens on the CPU with `scipy` anyways. What's surprising is the `result = B.solve(x)` line, which happens on the GPU, takes 9.86 s, which much slower (~120x slower) than the equivalent `scipy` step.

I tried to use linalg inv for a batch of small random matrices with streams. I observed the error that the outputs are filled with NANs and infs. 

In the code snipped, the inverse of the identity matrix is taken. In the first call, the output is correct, but not in the second call.
When rng is commented out the error does not occur. In addition, the error does not occur with additional device synchronization.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/86b5ce82-f7db-402a-95d6-0c6332bde686)

### To Reproduce

```py
import cupy as cp

def test_inv_stream(
    matrix_size,
    batch_size,
    dtype
):
    rng = cp.random.default_rng(seed=1)

    a_d = cp.empty((batch_size, matrix_size, matrix_size), dtype=dtype)

    # increase numerical stability
    for i in range(batch_size):
        a_d[i] = cp.eye(matrix_size, dtype=dtype)

    stream1 = cp.cuda.stream.Stream(non_blocking=True)
    
    stream1.synchronize()
    with stream1:
        inv_ref_d = cp.linalg.inv(a_d)
    stream1.synchronize()
    print(inv_ref_d)

test_inv_stream(5, 1, cp.float64)
test_inv_stream(10, 1, cp.float64)
```

Description

While using `cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu`, I noticed that subsequent `solve()` steps using the `SuperLU` result returned from `cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu` are a lot slower (~120x slower in the example below) than the equivalent `scipy` operation on the CPU. 

### To Reproduce

Here's the `scipy` version (note I'm using the ipython/jupyter `%time` magic for timing the `linalg.splu` and `.solve` lines):

```py
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import random, csc_matrix
from scipy.sparse import linalg

size = 10_000
A = random(size, size, density=0.5, random_state=2)
A = csc_matrix(A)
x = np.random.default_rng(seed=2).random(size)
%time B = linalg.splu(A)    # 1min 10s
%time result = B.solve(x)   # 81.5 ms
```

The output here gives a runtime of 1min 10s for the `B = linalg.splu(A)` line and 81.5 ms for the `result = B.solve(x)` line.

Switching to the equivalent `cupy` version:

```python
import cupy as cp
from cupyx.scipy.sparse import random, csc_matrix
from cupyx.scipy.sparse import linalg

size = 10_000
A = random(size, size, density=0.5, random_state=2)
A = csc_matrix(A)
x = cp.random.default_rng(seed=2).random(size)
%time B = linalg.splu(A)    # 1min 15s
%time result = B.solve(x)   # 9.86 s
```

In this case, the `B = linalg.splu(A)` line takes ~1min 15s , which is similar to the `scipy` CPU version. This is expected as the docs https://docs.cupy.dev/en/stable/reference/generated/cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu.html say that this step actually just happens on the CPU with `scipy` anyways. What's surprising is the `result = B.solve(x)` line, which happens on the GPU, takes 9.86 s, which much slower (~120x slower) than the equivalent `scipy` step.

Description

While using `cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu`, I noticed that subsequent `solve()` steps using the `SuperLU` result returned from `cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu` are a lot slower (~120x slower in the example below) than the equivalent `scipy` operation on the CPU. 

### To Reproduce

Here's the `scipy` version (note I'm using the ipython/jupyter `%time` magic for timing the `linalg.splu` and `.solve` lines):

```py
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import random, csc_matrix
from scipy.sparse import linalg

size = 10_000
A = random(size, size, density=0.5, random_state=2)
A = csc_matrix(A)
x = np.random.default_rng(seed=2).random(size)
%time B = linalg.splu(A)    # 1min 10s
%time result = B.solve(x)   # 81.5 ms
```

The output here gives a runtime of 1min 10s for the `B = linalg.splu(A)` line and 81.5 ms for the `result = B.solve(x)` line.

Switching to the equivalent `cupy` version:

```python
import cupy as cp
from cupyx.scipy.sparse import random, csc_matrix
from cupyx.scipy.sparse import linalg

size = 10_000
A = random(size, size, density=0.5, random_state=2)
A = csc_matrix(A)
x = cp.random.default_rng(seed=2).random(size)
%time B = linalg.splu(A)    # 1min 15s
%time result = B.solve(x)   # 9.86 s
```

In this case, the `B = linalg.splu(A)` line takes ~1min 15s , which is similar to the `scipy` CPU version. This is expected as the docs https://docs.cupy.dev/en/stable/reference/generated/cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.splu.html say that this step actually just happens on the CPU with `scipy` anyways. What's surprising is the `result = B.solve(x)` line, which happens on the GPU, takes 9.86 s, which much slower (~120x slower) than the equivalent `scipy` step.

In the code snipped, the inverse of the identity matrix is taken. In the first call, the output is correct, but not in the second call.
When rng is commented out the error does not occur. In addition, the error does not occur with additional device synchronization.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/86b5ce82-f7db-402a-95d6-0c6332bde686)

### To Reproduce

```py
import cupy as cp

def test_inv_stream(
    matrix_size,
    batch_size,
    dtype
):
    rng = cp.random.default_rng(seed=1)

    a_d = cp.empty((batch_size, matrix_size, matrix_size), dtype=dtype)

    # increase numerical stability
    for i in range(batch_size):
        a_d[i] = cp.eye(matrix_size, dtype=dtype)

    stream1 = cp.cuda.stream.Stream(non_blocking=True)
    
    stream1.synchronize()
    with stream1:
        inv_ref_d = cp.linalg.inv(a_d)
    stream1.synchronize()
    print(inv_ref_d)

test_inv_stream(5, 1, cp.float64)
test_inv_stream(10, 1, cp.float64)
```

Description

https://docs.cupy.dev/en/stable/reference/array_api.html recommends the use of the experimental `cupy.array_api` submodule as a mirror to the `numpy.array_api` experimental module.

In NumPy, the `numpy.array_api` experimental submodule introduced in 1.6 (or 1.5, I am not sure) has been removed in 2.0 as the top-level `numpy` module itself is expected to be array API compliant.

In scikit-learn, we test against both `cupy.array_api` and `cupy` directly via the `array_api_compat.cupy` wrapper. However `cupy.array_api` is not fully compliant with the latest version of the standard and we might need to invest efforts in maintaining our own wrapper (for instance to add the `clip` function). However we would rather not maintain a compat wrapper for something that is meant go away in the future.

### Idea or request for content


If cupy is to mirror numpy, then I would also expect the `cupy.array_api` submodule to go away in the future. If this is the case, I think it would be worth updating the doc to state this explicitly and instead point to `array_api_compat.cupy` as a pragmatic way for early array API users / consuming libraries It would be nice to have the support for cupy ufuncs on the array-like objects that define an `__array_ufunc__` method ([NEP-13](https://numpy.org/neps/nep-0013-ufunc-overrides.html))

Awkward knows how to dispatch through numpy ufuncs, and will dispatch to cupy ufuncs when encountering the "cuda" backend.

However, when using cupy ufuncs on awkward arrays with cuda backing it doesn't work out of the box!

Please, see the original discussion and a reproducer are here:
https://github.com/scikit-hep/awkward/issues/3232

also related to it:
https://github.com/NVIDIA/numba-cuda/issues/37

1. Don't forget to write a test code!

1. Build CuPy and run tests to confirm that the function runs fine:
  `pip install -e . && pytest tests/cupy_tests/PATH_TO_YOUR_TEST`
   See the [Contribution Guide](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/contribution.html#unit-testing) for details.

1. Submit a pull-request to the `main` branch.

+CuPy always raises ``NVRTC_ERROR_COMPILATION (6)``
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+
+On CUDA 12.2 or later, CUDA Runtime header files are required to compile kernels in CuPy.

This problem does not happen if you have installed CuPy from conda-forge (i.e., ``conda install -c conda-forge cupy``), as the package ``cuda-cudart-dev_<platform>`` that contains the needed headers is correctly installed as a dependency. Currently the same CCCL version is used at both build- and run- time, which is great for consistency. However, one missing step is every time the CCCL version is updated, we need a way to invalidate the kernel cache. A challenge in the cache invalidation, however, is we don't know which headers are actually used by the compiler, and to make it robust we might need to pay some run-time cost in attempting to mimic the compiler behavior, parse, and hash the used headers.

I am thinking we could start with something simpler, at the price of potentially more aggressive invalidation than needed. We can generate a hash at build time by extending the current `CUPY_CACHE_KEY` coverage to also cover the CCCL headers:
https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/9506efc49080c76a9662485e20cf7d95cd03394c/install/cupy_builder/_context.py#L60-L75
