Currently the same CCCL version is used at both build- and run- time, which is great for consistency. However, one missing step is every time the CCCL version is updated, we need a way to invalidate the kernel cache. A challenge in the cache invalidation, however, is we don't know which headers are actually used by the compiler, and to make it robust we might need to pay some run-time cost in attempting to mimic the compiler behavior, parse, and hash the used headers.

I am thinking we could start with something simpler, at the price of potentially more aggressive invalidation than needed. We can generate a hash at build time by extending the current `CUPY_CACHE_KEY` coverage to also cover the CCCL headers:
https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/9506efc49080c76a9662485e20cf7d95cd03394c/install/cupy_builder/_context.py#L60-L75
Since the same CCCL version is also used at run-time, this hash is valid. Then, we can dump this hash in, say, a json file that's shipped as part of the CuPy wheels and read in `cupy/cuda/_compiler.py` first time compiling a kernel in the process, and use it as part of the kernel cache key. Abstract

CUDA runtime provides a useful debug function [`cudaGraphDebugDotPrint()`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__GRAPH.html#group__CUDART__GRAPH_1gbec177c250000405c570dc8c4bde20db) for CUDA graphs.
This function can generate [DOT format](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html) file from `cudaGraph_t`.

This PR contains CuPy's wrapper of this function with the following APIs:

In `cupy.cuda.runtime`, 
- `graphDebugDotPrint(graph, path, flags)` function
- [`cudaGraphDebugDotFlags`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#group__CUDART__TYPES_1g0907ca7a1e7d0211b71ee49c5403072b) enums


In `cupy.cuda.Graph` class,
- `debug_dot_str(self, flags) -> str`: function to get debug DOT string

## Usage example

```python
import cupy
x = cupy.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
y = cupy.array([5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
st = cupy.cuda.Stream()
with st:
    st.begin_capture()
    x = x + y
    g = st.end_capture()

print(g.debug_dot_str(cupy.cuda.runtime.cudaGraphDebugDotFlagsVerbose))

Abstract

CUDA runtime provides a useful debug function [`cudaGraphDebugDotPrint()`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__GRAPH.html#group__CUDART__GRAPH_1gbec177c250000405c570dc8c4bde20db) for CUDA graphs.
This function can generate [DOT format](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html) file from `cudaGraph_t`.

This PR contains CuPy's wrapper of this function with the following APIs:

In `cupy.cuda.runtime`, 
- `graphDebugDotPrint(graph, path, flags)` function
- [`cudaGraphDebugDotFlags`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#group__CUDART__TYPES_1g0907ca7a1e7d0211b71ee49c5403072b) enums


In `cupy.cuda.Graph` class,
- `debug_dot_str(self, flags) -> str`: function to get debug DOT string

## Usage example

```python
import cupy
x = cupy.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
y = cupy.array([5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
st = cupy.cuda.Stream()
with st:
    st.begin_capture()
    x = x + y
    g = st.end_capture()

print(g.debug_dot_str(cupy.cuda.runtime.cudaGraphDebugDotFlagsVerbose))

Abstract

CUDA runtime provides a useful debug function [`cudaGraphDebugDotPrint()`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__GRAPH.html#group__CUDART__GRAPH_1gbec177c250000405c570dc8c4bde20db) for CUDA graphs.
This function can generate [DOT format](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html) file from `cudaGraph_t`.

This PR contains CuPy's wrapper of this function with the following APIs:

In `cupy.cuda.runtime`, 
- `graphDebugDotPrint(graph, path, flags)` function
- [`cudaGraphDebugDotFlags`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#group__CUDART__TYPES_1g0907ca7a1e7d0211b71ee49c5403072b) enums


In `cupy.cuda.Graph` class,
- `debug_dot_str(self, flags) -> str`: function to get debug DOT string

## Usage example

```python
import cupy
x = cupy.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
y = cupy.array([5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
st = cupy.cuda.Stream()
with st:
    st.begin_capture()
    x = x + y
    g = st.end_capture()

print(g.debug_dot_str(cupy.cuda.runtime.cudaGraphDebugDotFlagsVerbose))

Abstract

CUDA runtime provides a useful debug function [`cudaGraphDebugDotPrint()`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__GRAPH.html#group__CUDART__GRAPH_1gbec177c250000405c570dc8c4bde20db) for CUDA graphs.
This function can generate [DOT format](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html) file from `cudaGraph_t`.

This PR contains CuPy's wrapper of this function with the following APIs:

In `cupy.cuda.runtime`, 
- `graphDebugDotPrint(graph, path, flags)` function
- [`cudaGraphDebugDotFlags`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#group__CUDART__TYPES_1g0907ca7a1e7d0211b71ee49c5403072b) enums


In `cupy.cuda.Graph` class,
- `debug_dot_str(self, flags) -> str`: function to get debug DOT string

## Usage example

```python
import cupy
x = cupy.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
y = cupy.array([5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
st = cupy.cuda.Stream()
with st:
    st.begin_capture()
    x = x + y

Abstract

CUDA runtime provides a useful debug function [`cudaGraphDebugDotPrint()`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__GRAPH.html#group__CUDART__GRAPH_1gbec177c250000405c570dc8c4bde20db) for CUDA graphs.
This function can generate [DOT format](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html) file from `cudaGraph_t`.

This PR contains CuPy's wrapper of this function with the following APIs:

In `cupy.cuda.runtime`, 
- `graphDebugDotPrint(graph, path, flags)` function
- [`cudaGraphDebugDotFlags`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#group__CUDART__TYPES_1g0907ca7a1e7d0211b71ee49c5403072b) enums


In `cupy.cuda.Graph` class,
- `debug_dot_str(self, flags) -> str`: function to get debug DOT string

## Usage example

```python
import cupy
x = cupy.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
y = cupy.array([5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
st = cupy.cuda.Stream()
with st:
    st.begin_capture()
    x = x + y
    g = st.end_capture()

print(g.debug_dot_str(cupy.cuda.runtime.cudaGraphDebugDotFlagsVerbose))

Abstract

CUDA runtime provides a useful debug function [`cudaGraphDebugDotPrint()`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__GRAPH.html#group__CUDART__GRAPH_1gbec177c250000405c570dc8c4bde20db) for CUDA graphs.
This function can generate [DOT format](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html) file from `cudaGraph_t`.

This PR contains CuPy's wrapper of this function with the following APIs:

In `cupy.cuda.runtime`, 
- `graphDebugDotPrint(graph, path, flags)` function
- [`cudaGraphDebugDotFlags`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#group__CUDART__TYPES_1g0907ca7a1e7d0211b71ee49c5403072b) enums


In `cupy.cuda.Graph` class,
- `debug_dot_str(self, flags) -> str`: function to get debug DOT string

## Usage example

```python
import cupy
x = cupy.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
y = cupy.array([5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
st = cupy.cuda.Stream()
with st:
    st.begin_capture()
    x = x + y
    g = st.end_capture()

print(g.debug_dot_str(cupy.cuda.runtime.cudaGraphDebugDotFlagsVerbose))

Abstract

CUDA runtime provides a useful debug function [`cudaGraphDebugDotPrint()`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__GRAPH.html#group__CUDART__GRAPH_1gbec177c250000405c570dc8c4bde20db) for CUDA graphs.
This function can generate [DOT format](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html) file from `cudaGraph_t`.

This PR contains CuPy's wrapper of this function with the following APIs:

In `cupy.cuda.runtime`, 
- `graphDebugDotPrint(graph, path, flags)` function
- [`cudaGraphDebugDotFlags`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#group__CUDART__TYPES_1g0907ca7a1e7d0211b71ee49c5403072b) enums


In `cupy.cuda.Graph` class,
- `debug_dot_str(self, flags) -> str`: function to get debug DOT string

## Usage example

```python
import cupy
x = cupy.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
y = cupy.array([5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
st = cupy.cuda.Stream()
with st:
    st.begin_capture()
    x = x + y
    g = st.end_capture()

print(g.debug_dot_str(cupy.cuda.runtime.cudaGraphDebugDotFlagsVerbose))

Abstract

CUDA runtime provides a useful debug function [`cudaGraphDebugDotPrint()`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__GRAPH.html#group__CUDART__GRAPH_1gbec177c250000405c570dc8c4bde20db) for CUDA graphs.
This function can generate [DOT format](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html) file from `cudaGraph_t`.

This PR contains CuPy's wrapper of this function with the following APIs:

In `cupy.cuda.runtime`, 
- `graphDebugDotPrint(graph, path, flags)` function
- [`cudaGraphDebugDotFlags`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#group__CUDART__TYPES_1g0907ca7a1e7d0211b71ee49c5403072b) enums


In `cupy.cuda.Graph` class,
- `debug_dot_str(self, flags) -> str`: function to get debug DOT string

## Usage example

```python
import cupy
x = cupy.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
y = cupy.array([5, 6, 7, 8, 9])
st = cupy.cuda.Stream()
with st:
    st.begin_capture()
    x = x + y
    g = st.end_capture()

working on CuPy’s CUDA Graph conditional node support and considering adding a more user-friendly graph constructing API to CuPy.  
I have two possible plans to achieve this goal:

- (A) “with” API
- (B) Functional API

## (A) “with” API

### pseudo code

```python
import cupy
from contextlib import contextmanager

# Add conditional node to capturing graph and
# switch to different stream to capture body graph
@contextmanager
def while_loop():
    ...
@contextmanager
def if_else():
    ...

a: cupy.ndarray = ...
b: cupy.ndarray = ...

with capture_context() as ctx:
    ...
    with ctx.while_loop( # while loop
        cond_fn=lambda: cupy.all(a == b),
        cond_fn_args=() # Optional
    ):
        ... # while loop body

    with ctx.if_else(cond_fn=lambda: cupy.all(a != b)) as cond:
        with cond.if_():
            ...
        with cond.else_():
            # Should we consider `else` body support?
            # Currently conditional node does not support `else`
            # but seems to add support in the near future.
            ...

graph = ctx.get_graph() # get captured graph
graph.launch()
```

### Pros

- Considering the construction of CUDA graphs through stream capture, this approach provides a natural API.
- Allows for more concise writing of nested conditional nodes.

### Cons

- Defining a loop using the “with” syntax in Python may not be intuitive.
- Adding a support for an "else" body can result in an awkward or unnatural syntax.

## (B) Functional API

Is this the same approach with [torch.\_higher_order_ops.while](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/128544399441fa0ab32f2a95237212c911da5078/torch/_higher_order_ops/while_loop.py#L61-L114)?

### pseudo code

```python
# Prepare GraphConverter class to hold graph capturing state
class GraphConverter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.state = ... # need to have a global state

    # Function to define while loop
    def while_loop(self, cond_fn):
        def inner_func(body_fn, body_args=None):
            ... # operation to construct graph
        return inner_func

    def condition(self, cond_fn):
        def inner_func(true_fn, false_fn=None):
            ...
        return inner_func

    def convert(self, func):
        ...
        return func

gc = GraphConverter()
@gc.convert # A decorator to convert function to CUDA graph
def target(a: cupy.ndarray, b: cupy.ndarray):
    # While
    def while_fn(args):
        ...
    gc.while_loop(cond_fn=lambda: cupy.all(a == b))(while_fn, body_args)

    # You can also write as follows
    @gc.while_loop(cond_fn=lambda: cupy.all(a == b))
    def while_fn2():
        nonlocal a, b
        ...

    # if-then-else
    def true_fn():
        ...
    def false_fn():
        ...
    gc.condition(cond_fn)(
        true_fn=true_fn,
        false_fn=false_fn # easier to add `else` support
    )
    # or
    @gc.condition(cond_fn)
    def true_fn2():
        ...

target(a, b) # construct and execute graph at the same time
```

### Pros

- Simplifies the addition of "else" support when the conditional node supports an "else" body.
- Prevents issues related to unintentional variable overwriting and improper resource management, as functions naturally encapsulate variable scope.

### Cons

- Writing deeply nested programs can become complex and cumbersome, although using decorators can help alleviate this issue to some extent.
- Requires the use of the "nonlocal" declaration or passing variables as arguments to access outer-scope variables.

## Current status

I began implementing the API using the functional API approach (Plan B). However, switching to Plan A shouldn't be too time-consuming since the core implementation can be shared between both approaches.

I would like to ask your thoughts on these two ideas. Please let us know your preferences, potential advantages, pitfalls, and any other insights you might have.

A few drive-by comments:
1. I don't think we need to support `else` nodes, because without compiler help we have no way to validate if the user-provided `else` conditional function is strictly identical to the negate of the `if` counterpart. Users who need an `else` node should just write another `if` node.
2. Proposal A is fine with me if this is a concern:
> Defining a loop using the “with” syntax in Python may not be intuitive.

because in order to use stream capture to build a graph that contains conditional nodes, we have to walk through all the nodes at least once, unconditionally. The `with` syntax allows that. 

3. Proposal A's `ctx` usage to get a graph seems a bit odd to me. Usually after leaving the context manager, the context object is invalidated. (xref: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/8502#issuecomment-2311671823) But it is probably just a nitpick.
4. I don't like `gc` in Proposal B, as it could be confusing with the garbage collector. How about calling it, say, "GraphBuilder" (and aliasing it to `gb`)?
5. When using the decorator approach in Proposal B, such as `@gc.while_loop` and `gc.condition`, it seems to we still need to call `while_fn2` and `true_fn2` in `target` in order to have them executed at least once and captured. Is it an oversight?

In any approach, my biggest question is how you plan to generate additional kernels that take an `cudaGraphConditionalHandle` as argument and call `cudaGraphSetConditional` to set the value based on user-provided Python functions. There is some differences in cupyx.scipy's `lsmr()` and scipy's original `lsmr()` with their arguments.

CuPy
https://docs.cupy.dev/en/latest/reference/generated/cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.lsmr.html
```py
lsmr(A, b, x0=None, damp=0.0, atol=1e-06, btol=1e-06, conlim=100000000.0, maxiter=None)
```

SciPy
https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.linalg.lsmr.html
```py
lsmr(A, b, damp=0.0, atol=1e-06, btol=1e-06, conlim=100000000.0, maxiter=None, show=False, x0=None)
```

I found the following differences:

- Position of `x0`.
- CuPy's lsmr does not have `show` argument.
- When `maxiter=None` (default behavior), SciPy lsmr sets `maxiter=min(m, n)` (where (m, n) is the shape of A) automatically while CuPy's does not do so.

Currently the same CCCL version is used at both build- and run- time, which is great for consistency. However, one missing step is every time the CCCL version is updated, we need a way to invalidate the kernel cache. A challenge in the cache invalidation, however, is we don't know which headers are actually used by the compiler, and to make it robust we might need to pay some run-time cost in attempting to mimic the compiler behavior, parse, and hash the used headers.

I am thinking we could start with something simpler, at the price of potentially more aggressive invalidation than needed. We can generate a hash at build time by extending the current `CUPY_CACHE_KEY` coverage to also cover the CCCL headers:
https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/9506efc49080c76a9662485e20cf7d95cd03394c/install/cupy_builder/_context.py#L60-L75
Since the same CCCL version is also used at run-time, this hash is valid. Then, we can dump this hash in, say, a json file that's shipped as part of the CuPy wheels and read in `cupy/cuda/_compiler.py` first time compiling a kernel in the process, and use it as part of the kernel cache key. # Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run
* Make sure to cover the new Distutils C++ compilers

# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run
* Make sure to cover the new Distutils C++ compilers

# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run
* Make sure to cover the new Distutils C++ compilers

# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run
* Make sure to cover the new Distutils C++ compilers

# Background

Recently Leo added a patch to improve the Conda building experience in PR: https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7603 (which is fantastic as this was [a large patch in the cupy-feedstock]( https://github.com/conda-forge/cupy-feedstock/blob/6db86965e825788262d22a5f3c8b9aa6b93f9d96/recipe/support_new_cuda_layout.diff ). Thanks Leo! 🙏)

This worked ok in our testing of CuPy 13.3.0 builds (not to mention previous CuPy builds where we applied this patch in conda-forge). However (as later identified after further investigation), this broke due to the recently released Setuptools [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ).

In particular the breakage resulted in the following error [on CI]( https://dev.azure.com/conda-forge/feedstock-builds/_build/results?buildId=1007325&view=logs&j=d1321064-f6c3-56b7-0172-6d994d01c836&t=39022612-2533-571e-7b41-94814e7d38bb&l=1339 ):

```python
command 'c++' failed: No such file or directory
```

On the one hand this is a true statement as conda-forge intentional uses [a triple naming scheme with compilers and associated tools]( https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compilers-feedstock/blob/8853ee7c0d15a9a73b35503c384f5894cf38c379/recipe/get_cpu_arch.sh#L18-L31 ) to include the architecture, OS type, and OS version. So technically `c++` does not exist. However what it points to is that a command in Distutils is not using the conda-forge compilers during the build, which is the real problem. Reading the CI log led to this code in CuPy as where the error arose

<hr>

# Aligning compilers with the Python interpreter build

Most of the time when an error like this shows up with `distutils` the answer is to ensure [`distutils.sysconfig`'s `customize_compiler`]( https://docs.python.org/3.11/distutils/apiref.html#distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler ) is called on the new `CCompiler` object created by `distutils`. What this does (as the legacy `distutils` documentation in Python 3.11 linked above explains), is update the `distutils` `CCompiler` object based on settings used to build Python itself. IOW in conda-forge `python` is also built with conda-forge's compiler toolchain. So residual information from that build experience lives in the `python` package conda-forge produces. Thus `customize_compiler` then updates `CCompiler` to work with the conda-forge toolchain. Should add `customize_compiler` only does something in the UNIX case currently (it could potentially be updated to do something on Windows). This would be done by a change like that shown below. Normally this would be enough

```diff
     compiler = ccompiler.new_compiler()
+    distutils.sysconfig.customize_compiler(compiler)
```

<hr>

# Handling cross-compilers

However as the goal of the logic in this part of the CuPy code base is to build an artifact for the native platform and inspect it, that won't work with these compiler settings. Why is that? Well conda-forge uses a cross-compiling toolchain. Meaning the compilers are able to perform a build on a different platform than where the final package will be deployed. So building on Linux `x86_64` (plentiful in the world of CI currently) to create packages for Linux ARM (less available currently). IOW this is done to balance resource availability with user demand. So calling `customize_compiler` in conda-forge actually configures the compiler to target the platform where packages will be deployed (called `host_platform`). However for CuPy's use case here, we need to target `build_platform`, which may be different

As a result a manual patch is needed to configure the build tools for `build_platform`. The logic Leo added here did that based on [what `distutils` had in Python 3.11]( https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/795f2597a4be988e2bb19b69ff9958e981cb894e/Lib/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L49-L63 ). So what were we missing that resulted in new errors?

<hr>

# Setuptools, Distutils & the evolving Python packaging landscape

For a long time now, `setuptools` has monkeypatched `distutils`. In the past this meant there needed to be a specific `import` order for this to work. Namely `setuptools` first and then `distutils`. Though this caused some consternation for users and maintainers ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/2259 ). So `setuptools` changed this to always prefer its own vendored `distutils` ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/2305 ). Why does this matter? Well it means we never actually get `distutils` from the Python stdlib. We always get it from what `setuptools` vendored. This also explains why upstream removing its copy of `distutils` in Python 3.12 (please see [PEP 632]( https://peps.python.org/pep-0632 )) did not affect us (as we were not using it)

Though why do we care how `setuptools` supplies `distutils`. Well that [source code lives outside CPython]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils ) and we get updates whenever `setuptools` refreshes [its vendored `distutils`]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/tree/v72.0.0/setuptools/_distutils ). IOW just because the `distutils` source is updated doesn't mean it will be in `setuptools` yet. The vendored copy needs to be refreshed as well, which may happen out-of-sync relative to the `distutils` source. These pieces are important when trying to make sense of changes to `distutils` and how/when they will affect us

<hr>

# Distutils learns about C++ compilers

So what changed in `distutils`? Earlier this year `distutils` included updates for C++ compiler handling via PR ( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/pull/228 ). This expanded [the executables in `CCompiler`]( https://github.com/pypa/distutils/blob/fcef96367a0aef5bcf58027553ca36d50805210c/distutils/unixccompiler.py#L111-L129 ) by adding a C++ equivalent executable for every C associated one previously. This actually improves working with C++ compilers in `distutils`, which is pretty important for CUDA as well. So this is a helpful fix

<hr>

# Software supply chains and their logistics

Even though that `distutils` improvement went in at the beginning of August, we did not see it right away. This is because Setuptools refreshed `distutils` a week later with PR ( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4539 ). The next Setuptools release, [72.2.0]( https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/releases/tag/v72.2.0 ), was a week after that (so 2 weeks after the `distutils` PR was merged). Then conda-forge waited a week to confirm there were not user errors showing up before shipping ( https://github.com/conda-forge/setuptools-feedstock/pull/355 ). So we only started seeing this error 3 weeks after the `distutils` change

<hr>

# Resolution

In any event, now that we have learned about these changes and understood the source, we can apply an appropriate patch. Namely...

* Configure the `distutils` `CCompiler` to match how Python is built
* Patch toolchain to target the build machine where it is run
* Make sure to cover the new Distutils C++ compilers

Currently the same CCCL version is used at both build- and run- time, which is great for consistency. However, one missing step is every time the CCCL version is updated, we need a way to invalidate the kernel cache. A challenge in the cache invalidation, however, is we don't know which headers are actually used by the compiler, and to make it robust we might need to pay some run-time cost in attempting to mimic the compiler behavior, parse, and hash the used headers.

I am thinking we could start with something simpler, at the price of potentially more aggressive invalidation than needed. We can generate a hash at build time by extending the current `CUPY_CACHE_KEY` coverage to also cover the CCCL headers:
https://github.com/cupy/cupy/blob/9506efc49080c76a9662485e20cf7d95cd03394c/install/cupy_builder/_context.py#L60-L75
Since the same CCCL version is also used at run-time, this hash is valid. Then, we can dump this hash in, say, a json file that's shipped as part of the CuPy wheels and read in `cupy/cuda/_compiler.py` first time compiling a kernel in the process, and use it as part of the kernel cache key. edit: This PR adopts recent setuptools changes, specifically v74.0.0 (which [removed](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4600) `setuptools.msvc`) and v74.1.0+ (which [reverted](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/pull/4626) `setuptools.msvc` but requires explicit module import instead of `import setuptools`).

<details>
<summary>Original description</summary>

On Windows platform with setuptools 74+, it will now take 2-3 seconds to find `cl.exe`. This overhead happens only once per process, and only when the use of `nvcc` is requested.

`setuptools.msvc` (which we rely on for years and is now removed) was able to discover `cl.exe` very quickly as it directly reads the Windows registry. The new approach introduced in this PR (which only uses the public/documented setuptools API) retrives the compiler path through `vcvarsall.bat`, which incurs subprocess invocation.

Hi all - first-time contributor here, so I went to https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/6078#issue-1051191869 and picked an API under the Easy category to implement: `numpy.ndarray.itemset`. In line with the recommendation in the [Contribution Guide](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/stable/contribution.html#issues-and-pull-requests) to submit an issue for new APIs, I'm creating this post to discuss the design.

tl;dr - Two questions: should the code be contained in `cupy._core.core.pyx`? Since it's modifying on-device arrays, should it have its own kernel or make use of others that could do the job?

I found the TODO that (in theory) marks where the function should go in `cupy._core.core.pyx`. Looking at other similar functions there which modify data on the GPU, it seems there are two standard implementations. The first is to expose a method in `_ndarray_base` which calls a kernel (e.g. `_ndarray_base.fill`). The second is to expose a method in `_ndarray_base` which calls to another method in a different `_routines_*.pyx` file. **Organizationally speaking, is there another `.pyx` file where the private implementation of `ndarray.itemset` should live**? It's a simple enough function that I think it would make sense for it to just live in `core.pyx`, but I'm not sure what the precedent is.

Looking at the expected behavior of `numpy.ndarray.itemset`, it seems like the only mode of operation is modifying a singular value in the ndarray. This brings me to my next question - for this simple of a function, **is a dedicated kernel necessary or can I make use of another pre-existing kernel?** There are a few other methods that would already provide the abstraction of "set some elements in an on-device array to some value," so that could potentially also work for `ndarray.itemset`.

Description

Hi all - first-time contributor here, so I went to https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/6078#issue-1051191869 and picked an API under the Easy category to implement: `numpy.ndarray.itemset`. In line with the recommendation in the [Contribution Guide](https://docs.cupy.dev/en/stable/contribution.html#issues-and-pull-requests) to submit an issue for new APIs, I'm creating this post to discuss the design.

tl;dr - Two questions: should the code be contained in `cupy._core.core.pyx`? Since it's modifying on-device arrays, should it have its own kernel or make use of others that could do the job?

I found the TODO that (in theory) marks where the function should go in `cupy._core.core.pyx`. Looking at other similar functions there which modify data on the GPU, it seems there are two standard implementations. The first is to expose a method in `_ndarray_base` which calls a kernel (e.g. `_ndarray_base.fill`). The second is to expose a method in `_ndarray_base` which calls to another method in a different `_routines_*.pyx` file. **Organizationally speaking, is there another `.pyx` file where the private implementation of `ndarray.itemset` should live**? It's a simple enough function that I think it would make sense for it to just live in `core.pyx`, but I'm not sure what the precedent is.

Looking at the expected behavior of `numpy.ndarray.itemset`, it seems like the only mode of operation is modifying a singular value in the ndarray. This brings me to my next question - for this simple of a function, **is a dedicated kernel necessary or can I make use of another pre-existing kernel?** There are a few other methods that would already provide the abstraction of "set some elements in an on-device array to some value," so that could potentially also work for `ndarray.itemset`.

working on CuPy’s CUDA Graph conditional node support and considering adding a more user-friendly graph constructing API to CuPy.  
I have two possible plans to achieve this goal:

- (A) “with” API
- (B) Functional API

## (A) “with” API

### pseudo code

```python
import cupy
from contextlib import contextmanager

# Add conditional node to capturing graph and
# switch to different stream to capture body graph
@contextmanager
def while_loop():
    ...
@contextmanager
def if_else():
    ...

a: cupy.ndarray = ...
b: cupy.ndarray = ...

with capture_context() as ctx:
    ...
    with ctx.while_loop( # while loop
        cond_fn=lambda: cupy.all(a == b),
        cond_fn_args=() # Optional
    ):
        ... # while loop body

    with ctx.if_else(cond_fn=lambda: cupy.all(a != b)) as cond:
        with cond.if_():
            ...
        with cond.else_():
            # Should we consider `else` body support?
            # Currently conditional node does not support `else`
            # but seems to add support in the near future.
            ...

graph = ctx.get_graph() # get captured graph
graph.launch()
```

### Pros

- Considering the construction of CUDA graphs through stream capture, this approach provides a natural API.
- Allows for more concise writing of nested conditional nodes.

### Cons

- Defining a loop using the “with” syntax in Python may not be intuitive.
- Adding a support for an "else" body can result in an awkward or unnatural syntax.

## (B) Functional API

Is this the same approach with [torch.\_higher_order_ops.while](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/128544399441fa0ab32f2a95237212c911da5078/torch/_higher_order_ops/while_loop.py#L61-L114)?

### pseudo code

```python
# Prepare GraphConverter class to hold graph capturing state
class GraphConverter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.state = ... # need to have a global state

    # Function to define while loop
    def while_loop(self, cond_fn):
        def inner_func(body_fn, body_args=None):
            ... # operation to construct graph
        return inner_func

    def condition(self, cond_fn):
        def inner_func(true_fn, false_fn=None):
            ...
        return inner_func

    def convert(self, func):
        ...
        return func

gc = GraphConverter()
@gc.convert # A decorator to convert function to CUDA graph
def target(a: cupy.ndarray, b: cupy.ndarray):
    # While
    def while_fn(args):
        ...
    gc.while_loop(cond_fn=lambda: cupy.all(a == b))(while_fn, body_args)

    # You can also write as follows
    @gc.while_loop(cond_fn=lambda: cupy.all(a == b))
    def while_fn2():
        nonlocal a, b
        ...

    # if-then-else
    def true_fn():
        ...
    def false_fn():
        ...
    gc.condition(cond_fn)(
        true_fn=true_fn,
        false_fn=false_fn # easier to add `else` support
    )
    # or
    @gc.condition(cond_fn)
    def true_fn2():
        ...

target(a, b) # construct and execute graph at the same time
```

### Pros

- Simplifies the addition of "else" support when the conditional node supports an "else" body.
- Prevents issues related to unintentional variable overwriting and improper resource management, as functions naturally encapsulate variable scope.

### Cons

- Writing deeply nested programs can become complex and cumbersome, although using decorators can help alleviate this issue to some extent.
- Requires the use of the "nonlocal" declaration or passing variables as arguments to access outer-scope variables.

## Current status

I began implementing the API using the functional API approach (Plan B). However, switching to Plan A shouldn't be too time-consuming since the core implementation can be shared between both approaches.

I would like to ask your thoughts on these two ideas. Please let us know your preferences, potential advantages, pitfalls, and any other insights you might have.

Description

I've been working on getting CuPy to compile on a cluster with AMD GPUs which has ROCm 6.1.1 (see https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/8585 for related issue) and there are a number of places in the code for CuPy where for HIP devices it refers to things are were previously deprecated and are now removed in 6.x

Specifically:

`hipMemoryTypeDevice` and `hipMemoryTypeHost` no longer have an attribute `memoryType` but follow Cuda in having `type` instead. (https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/cupy_hip_runtime.h.patch + https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/_runtime_typedef.pxi.patch, https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/runtime.pyx.patch)

`gcnArch` has now also been removed (https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/runtime.pyx.patch)

My patches are messy so someone should probably take a proper look at this and fix it for future releases.


### To Reproduce

Compile CuPy 13.3.0 on ROCm 6.1.1

### Installation

None

### Environment

N/A

Description

I've been working on getting CuPy to compile on a cluster with AMD GPUs which has ROCm 6.1.1 (see https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/8585 for related issue) and there are a number of places in the code for CuPy where for HIP devices it refers to things are were previously deprecated and are now removed in 6.x

Specifically:

`hipMemoryTypeDevice` and `hipMemoryTypeHost` no longer have an attribute `memoryType` but follow Cuda in having `type` instead. (https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/cupy_hip_runtime.h.patch + https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/_runtime_typedef.pxi.patch, https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/runtime.pyx.patch)

`gcnArch` has now also been removed (https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/runtime.pyx.patch)

My patches are messy so someone should probably take a proper look at this and fix it for future releases.


### To Reproduce

Compile CuPy 13.3.0 on ROCm 6.1.1

### Installation

None

### Environment

N/A

### To Reproduce

1. Create a new virtualenvironment on a system with ROCm 6.x
2. Install latest setuptools (74.1.1) from pip
3. Set environment variables.

```
export ROCM_HOME=/opt/rocm
export HCC_AMDGPU_TARGET=gfx90a
export CFLAGS="-I/opt/rocm/include/hipblas -I/opt/rocm/include/hipsparse -I/opt/rocm/include/hipfft -I/opt/rocm/include/rocsolver -I/opt/rocm/include/rccl"
```

4. Either `pip install cupy` or clone the source and run `python3 setup.py bdist_wheel`

Description

I've been working on getting CuPy to compile on a cluster with AMD GPUs which has ROCm 6.1.1 (see https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/8585 for related issue) and there are a number of places in the code for CuPy where for HIP devices it refers to things are were previously deprecated and are now removed in 6.x

Specifically:

`hipMemoryTypeDevice` and `hipMemoryTypeHost` no longer have an attribute `memoryType` but follow Cuda in having `type` instead. (https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/cupy_hip_runtime.h.patch + https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/_runtime_typedef.pxi.patch, https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/runtime.pyx.patch)

`gcnArch` has now also been removed (https://github.com/owainkenwayucl/boyd/blob/master/billets/cupy/patches/runtime.pyx.patch)

My patches are messy so someone should probably take a proper look at this and fix it for future releases.


### To Reproduce

Compile CuPy 13.3.0 on ROCm 6.1.1

None

In numpy, you can use `==` and `!=` to check which item in an `ndarray` is None.
In cupy, comparing an array to None raises `NotImplemented`.

Numpy example:
```
import numpy as np
>>> a = np.array([1, 2, None])
>>> a == None
array([False, False,  True])
```

Cupy example:
```
import cupy
>>> a = cupy.array([1, 2, cupy.nan])
>>> a == None
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "cupy/_core/core.pyx", line 1217, in cupy._core.core._ndarray_base.__richcmp__
TypeError: operand type(s) all returned NotImplemented from __array_ufunc__(<ufunc 'equal'>, '__call__', array([ 1.,  2., nan]), None): 'ndarray', 'NoneType'
```

Notice that numpy checks equality against `None` and not against `np.nan`
